blocks.body:
The Riemann hypothesis says that every nontrivial zero of $\zeta(s)$ has real part exactly $\tfrac12$. Nobody can prove it, but for most applications to primes the full statement is not needed. What does the damage is a zero $\rho=\beta+i\gamma$ with $\beta$ close to $1$: through the [[explicit-formula|explicit formula]] it puts a term of size $x^{\beta}$ into $\psi(x)$. A zero-density estimate says that such zeros, if they exist at all, are rare, and the further right you go the rarer they must be.

This lesson defines the counting function $N(\sigma,T)$, explains what shape of bound one can hope for, proves a first density theorem from a mean-value estimate, and shows how density bounds give primes in short intervals.

blocks.title: The zero-counting function N(σ, T)
blocks.body:
For $\tfrac12\le\sigma\le 1$ and $T\ge 2$ put
$$N(\sigma,T)=\#\{\rho=\beta+i\gamma:\ \zeta(\rho)=0,\ \beta\ge\sigma,\ 0<\gamma\le T\},$$
counting zeros with multiplicity. A density estimate is a bound of the form
$$N(\sigma,T)\ll T^{A(1-\sigma)}(\log T)^B\qquad\text{uniformly for } \tfrac12\le\sigma\le1,$$
or the slightly weaker $N(\sigma,T)\ll_\varepsilon T^{A(1-\sigma)+\varepsilon}$.

In words: $N(\sigma,T)$ counts the zeros in the box to the right of the vertical line $\mathrm{Re}\,s=\sigma$ up to height $T$, and the Riemann hypothesis is exactly the statement that $N(\sigma,T)=0$ for every $\sigma>\tfrac12$.

blocks.title: What shape of bound to expect
blocks.body:
Look first at the two ends of the range.

At $\sigma=\tfrac12$: by the Riemann–von Mangoldt formula ([[nontrivial-zeros]]) the total number of zeros with $0<\gamma\le T$ is $N(T)=\frac{T}{2\pi}\log\frac{T}{2\pi}-\frac{T}{2\pi}+O(\log T)$. The map $\rho\mapsto 1-\bar\rho$ sends nontrivial zeros to nontrivial zeros, keeps the ordinate $\gamma$ and swaps $\beta$ with $1-\beta$. So at least half of all zeros have $\beta\ge\tfrac12$, and $N(\tfrac12,T)\ge \tfrac12N(T)\gg T\log T$.

At $\sigma=1$: there are no zeros on the line $\mathrm{Re}\,s=1$, so $N(1,T)=0$. The [[zero-free-region|zero-free region]] gives more: $N(\sigma,T)=0$ once $\sigma\ge 1-c/\log T$.

A bound $T^{A(1-\sigma)}$ interpolates between these: the exponent falls linearly from $A/2$ at $\sigma=\tfrac12$ to $0$ at $\sigma=1$. Since the left side is at least of size $T\log T$ at $\sigma=\tfrac12$, no such bound can hold with $A<2$. The density hypothesis is the conjecture that $A=2$ is admissible:
$$N(\sigma,T)\ll_\varepsilon T^{2(1-\sigma)+\varepsilon}.$$
It follows from the Riemann hypothesis trivially and from the [[lindelof|Lindelöf hypothesis]] by a theorem of Ingham.

Uniformity in $\sigma$ matters because applications integrate over $\sigma$: a zero with real part $\beta$ costs $x^{\beta-1}$ relative to the main term, and the bound must beat that cost for every $\beta$ at once.

blocks.title: The main density theorems
blocks.body:
1. Bohr and Landau (1914): for each fixed $\sigma>\tfrac12$, $N(\sigma,T)=O_\sigma(T)$.
2. Carlson (1920): $N(\sigma,T)\ll_\varepsilon T^{4\sigma(1-\sigma)+\varepsilon}$.
3. Ingham (1940): $N(\sigma,T)\ll T^{3(1-\sigma)/(2-\sigma)}(\log T)^5$. Since $3/(2-\sigma)\le 3$, this gives $A=3$.
4. Huxley (1972): $N(\sigma,T)\ll T^{3(1-\sigma)/(3\sigma-1)}(\log T)^B$ for $\tfrac34\le\sigma\le1$. Combined with Ingham's bound for $\sigma\le\tfrac34$ (the two exponents agree at $\sigma=\tfrac34$, where both equal $\tfrac{12}{5}(1-\sigma)$), this gives $A=\tfrac{12}{5}$.
5. Guth and Maynard (2024): $N(\sigma,T)\ll_\varepsilon T^{15(1-\sigma)/(3+5\sigma)+\varepsilon}$, which beats the older bounds for $\tfrac{7}{10}<\sigma<\tfrac{8}{10}$. Combined with Ingham and Huxley this gives $A=\tfrac{30}{13}$ (with an $\varepsilon$).

The density hypothesis $A=2$ remains open; it is known only for $\sigma$ sufficiently close to $1$ (Huxley's bound alone gives it for $\sigma\ge\tfrac56$, where $3/(3\sigma-1)\le2$).

blocks.title: Zeros are detected by mean values
blocks.body:
Why should averages of $|\zeta|$ say anything about zeros? Jensen's formula from complex analysis already says that the number of zeros of a holomorphic function in a disc is controlled by the average of $\log|f|$ on a larger circle. For rectangles there is a version adapted to counting zeros by their real parts.

Littlewood's lemma. Let $f$ be holomorphic on an open set containing the rectangle $R=\{\sigma_0\le\mathrm{Re}\,s\le\sigma_1,\ t_0\le\mathrm{Im}\,s\le T\}$, with no zeros on the boundary of $R$. For $\sigma_0\le u\le\sigma_1$ let $\nu(u)$ be the number of zeros of $f$ in $R$ with real part greater than $u$. Then
$$2\pi\int_{\sigma_0}^{\sigma_1}\nu(u)\,du=\int_{t_0}^{T}\log|f(\sigma_0+it)|\,dt-\int_{t_0}^{T}\log|f(\sigma_1+it)|\,dt+\int_{\sigma_0}^{\sigma_1}\arg f(u+iT)\,du-\int_{\sigma_0}^{\sigma_1}\arg f(u+it_0)\,du,$$
where $\arg f$ on the horizontal sides is defined by continuous variation starting from the right-hand side.

The idea of the proof: cut $R$ along horizontal segments running left from each zero to the left edge, so that $\log f$ has a single-valued branch on what remains, and integrate $\log f$ around the boundary. Across the cut from a zero $\beta+i\gamma$ the logarithm jumps by $2\pi i$, and the cut has length $\beta-\sigma_0$; the cuts contribute $2\pi\sum(\beta-\sigma_0)$, which equals $2\pi\int_{\sigma_0}^{\sigma_1}\nu(u)\,du$. Comparing imaginary parts gives the formula. We omit the details (see Titchmarsh, Chapter IX).

The useful feature is that the left edge enters only through $\int\log|f|$, and by concavity of the logarithm this is bounded by the logarithm of a mean square. Mean squares of $\zeta$ are exactly what the theory of [[moments]] provides.

blocks.title: A first density bound
blocks.body:
Fix $\tfrac12<\sigma_0<\sigma<1$, with $\sigma_0$ chosen so that no zero of $\zeta$ has real part exactly $\sigma_0$ (this excludes only countably many values). Then as $T\to\infty$
$$N(\sigma,T)\le\Bigl(\frac{\log\zeta(2\sigma_0)}{4\pi(\sigma-\sigma_0)}+o(1)\Bigr)T.$$
In particular $N(\sigma,T)=O_\sigma(T)$ for every fixed $\sigma>\tfrac12$, while $N(T)\sim\frac{T}{2\pi}\log T$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
We use two standard facts. First, the mean value theorem: for fixed $\sigma_0>\tfrac12$,
$$\frac1T\int_1^T|\zeta(\sigma_0+it)|^2\,dt\to\zeta(2\sigma_0)\qquad(T\to\infty).$$
Second, $\arg\zeta(u+iT)=O(\log T)$ uniformly for $u\ge\tfrac12$ when $T$ is not the ordinate of a zero (this is the bound behind the error term in the Riemann–von Mangoldt formula). It is enough to treat such $T$: for any $T$, apply the result at a slightly larger admissible $T'$, which only increases $N(\sigma,\cdot)$.

Apply Littlewood's lemma to $f=\zeta$ on the rectangle $\sigma_0\le\mathrm{Re}\,s\le2$, $1\le\mathrm{Im}\,s\le T$. The pole $s=1$ lies outside it; there are no zeros with ordinate in $(0,1]$ (the lowest is near $14.13$), none with real part $\ge1$, and none on the left edge by the choice of $\sigma_0$. So for $\sigma_0\le u\le2$, $\nu(u)$ counts zeros with $\beta>u$ and $0<\gamma\le T$.

Right edge. For $\mathrm{Re}\,s>1$, $\log\zeta(s)=\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\Lambda(n)}{\log n}n^{-s}$, so
$$\int_1^T\log|\zeta(2+it)|\,dt=\mathrm{Re}\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\Lambda(n)}{n^2\log n}\int_1^Tn^{-it}\,dt,$$
and $|\int_1^Tn^{-it}dt|\le 2/\log n$. The sum converges, so this term is $O(1)$.

Horizontal edges. The top contributes $O(\log T)$ by the second fact; the bottom is a fixed number.

Left edge. Since $\log$ is concave, Jensen's inequality gives
$$\int_1^T\log|\zeta(\sigma_0+it)|\,dt=\frac12\int_1^T\log|\zeta(\sigma_0+it)|^2\,dt\le\frac{T-1}{2}\log\Bigl(\frac{1}{T-1}\int_1^T|\zeta(\sigma_0+it)|^2dt\Bigr)=\frac T2\bigl(\log\zeta(2\sigma_0)+o(1)\bigr).$$

Putting the pieces together,
$$2\pi\int_{\sigma_0}^{2}\nu(u)\,du\le\frac T2\log\zeta(2\sigma_0)+o(T).$$
Now every zero counted by $N(\sigma,T)$ has $\beta\ge\sigma>u$ for each $u\in[\sigma_0,\sigma)$, so $\nu(u)\ge N(\sigma,T)$ there, and $\nu\ge0$ everywhere. Hence $\int_{\sigma_0}^2\nu\ge(\sigma-\sigma_0)N(\sigma,T)$, and dividing by $2\pi(\sigma-\sigma_0)$ gives $N(\sigma,T)\le\bigl(\frac{\log\zeta(2\sigma_0)}{4\pi(\sigma-\sigma_0)}+o(1)\bigr)T$, which is the theorem.

Taking $\sigma_0$ near $(\sigma+\tfrac12)/2$ gives the clean form $N(\sigma,T)\le\bigl(\frac{\log\zeta(\sigma+1/2)}{2\pi(\sigma-1/2)}+o(1)\bigr)T$. Comparing with $N(T)\sim\frac{T}{2\pi}\log T$: the proportion of zeros with $\beta\ge\sigma$ is $O_\sigma(1/\log T)$.

blocks.title: From O(T) to a power saving: mollifiers and large values
blocks.body:
The argument above is wasteful: $|\zeta|^2$ has mean $\zeta(2\sigma_0)>1$. The stronger theorems first multiply $\zeta$ by a mollifier
$$M_X(s)=\sum_{n\le X}\frac{\mu(n)}{n^{s}},$$
a truncation of $1/\zeta(s)$. Then $\zeta(s)M_X(s)=1+\sum_{n>X}a_nn^{-s}$, where $a_n=\sum_{d\mid n,\ d\le X}\mu(d)$ vanishes for $2\le n\le X$ (Example 4). At a zero $\rho$ the left side is $0$, so the tail $\sum_{n>X}a_n n^{-\rho}$ must equal $-1$: a zero forces a Dirichlet polynomial (after smoothing and shifting the line of integration) to take a large value.

So zero-density becomes a question about large values: given a Dirichlet polynomial $D(t)=\sum_{N<n\le2N}b_nn^{-it}$ and a threshold $V$, how many well-spaced points $t_1,\dots,t_R\in[0,T]$ can have $|D(t_r)|\ge V$? The mean value theorem for Dirichlet polynomials,
$$\int_0^T\Bigl|\sum_{n\le N}b_nn^{-it}\Bigr|^2dt=\sum_{n\le N}(T+O(n))|b_n|^2,$$
due to Montgomery and Vaughan and a relative of the [[large-sieve|large sieve]], gives $R\ll(T+N)\sum|b_n|^2/V^2$ up to logarithms. Ingham's theorem comes essentially from this together with the fourth moment of $\zeta$. Huxley's improvement uses the Halász–Montgomery large values inequality, which does better when $R$ is large. The Guth–Maynard bound comes from a new large values estimate that is strongest near the critical point $\sigma=\tfrac34$ where the older bounds were weakest. In every case the bound is optimised by choosing the mollifier length $X$ and the polynomial lengths as powers of $T$ depending on $\sigma$, which is why the exponents are rational functions of $\sigma$.

blocks.title: Why density is almost as good as RH: primes in short intervals
blocks.body:
The truncated explicit formula ([[explicit-formula]]) says that for $2\le T\le x$
$$\psi(x)=x-\sum_{|\gamma|\le T}\frac{x^{\rho}}{\rho}+O\Bigl(\frac{x}{T}(\log x)^2\Bigr).$$
Subtract the same formula at $x$ from the one at $x+h$. Since $\frac{(x+h)^\rho-x^\rho}{\rho}=\int_x^{x+h}u^{\rho-1}du$ and $|u^{\rho-1}|=u^{\beta-1}\le x^{\beta-1}$,
$$\bigl|\psi(x+h)-\psi(x)-h\bigr|\le h\sum_{|\gamma|\le T}x^{\beta-1}+O\Bigl(\frac{x}{T}(\log x)^2\Bigr).$$
Take $h=x^{\theta}$ and $T=x^{1-\theta+\delta}$ with small $\delta>0$; then the error term is $o(h)$. It remains to show $\sum_{|\gamma|\le T}x^{\beta-1}=o(1)$. Writing $x^{\beta-1}=x^{-1/2}+\int_{1/2}^{\beta}x^{u-1}\log x\,du$ for $\beta\ge\tfrac12$ and using $x^{\beta-1}\le x^{-1/2}$ for $\beta<\tfrac12$,
$$\sum_{|\gamma|\le T}x^{\beta-1}\ll x^{-1/2}\,T\log T+\log x\int_{1/2}^{1}x^{u-1}N(u,T)\,du.$$
The first term is small because $T<x^{1/2-\delta}$ once $\theta>\tfrac12+2\delta$. In the integral, a density bound gives $x^{u-1}N(u,T)\ll(T^A/x)^{1-u}(\log T)^B$. If $T^A\le x^{1-\delta'}$ this is at most $x^{-\delta'(1-u)}(\log T)^B$, and the zero-free region means only $1-u\ge\eta(T)$ matters, where the Vinogradov–Korobov region has $\eta(T)=c(\log T)^{-2/3}(\log\log T)^{-1/3}$. Then $x^{-\delta'\eta(T)}$ decays faster than any power of $\log x$, and the integral is $o(1)$.

The condition $T^A<x^{1-\delta'}$ with $T=x^{1-\theta+\delta}$ means $A(1-\theta)<1$, that is $\theta>1-1/A$.

blocks.title: Density bounds give primes in short intervals
blocks.body:
Suppose $N(\sigma,T)\ll T^{A(1-\sigma)}(\log T)^B$ uniformly for $\tfrac12\le\sigma\le1$. Then for every fixed $\theta>1-\frac1A$,
$$\psi(x+x^{\theta})-\psi(x)\sim x^{\theta}\qquad(x\to\infty),$$
and consequently $p_{n+1}-p_n\ll p_n^{\theta}$.

With Huxley's $A=\tfrac{12}{5}$ this gives $\theta>\tfrac{7}{12}$. Guth and Maynard deduced the corresponding result for every $\theta>\tfrac{17}{30}$. The density hypothesis would give every $\theta>\tfrac12$; RH gives a little more, namely intervals of length $\sqrt x(\log x)^{2+\varepsilon}$, because under RH $\psi(x+h)-\psi(x)=h+O(\sqrt x(\log x)^2)$.

blocks.title: Example 1: bookkeeping with exponents
blocks.body:
(a) Check that Ingham's and Huxley's exponents agree at $\sigma=\tfrac34$, and that the Guth–Maynard exponent agrees with Ingham's at $\sigma=\tfrac7{10}$ and with Huxley's at $\sigma=\tfrac8{10}$.

(b) For $A=3,\ \tfrac{12}{5},\ \tfrac{30}{13},\ 2$, compute the short-interval exponent $1-1/A$.
blocks.solution:
(a) Divide each exponent by $1-\sigma$. Ingham: $3/(2-\sigma)$; Huxley: $3/(3\sigma-1)$; Guth–Maynard: $15/(3+5\sigma)$. At $\sigma=\tfrac34$: $3/(5/4)=\tfrac{12}{5}$ and $3/(5/4)=\tfrac{12}5$. At $\sigma=\tfrac7{10}$: $3/(13/10)=\tfrac{30}{13}$ and $15/(13/2)=\tfrac{30}{13}$. At $\sigma=\tfrac8{10}$: $15/7$ and $3/(7/5)=\tfrac{15}{7}$. Ingham's ratio increases with $\sigma$ and the other two decrease, so on $[\tfrac12,1]$ the best available ratio is largest at the crossing points: $\tfrac{12}5$ at $\tfrac34$ without Guth–Maynard, and $\tfrac{30}{13}$ at $\tfrac7{10}$ with it.

(b) $1-\tfrac13=\tfrac23$; $1-\tfrac5{12}=\tfrac7{12}$; $1-\tfrac{13}{30}=\tfrac{17}{30}$; $1-\tfrac12=\tfrac12$. In decimals: $0.667,\ 0.583,\ 0.567,\ 0.5$.

blocks.title: Example 2: why A cannot be smaller than 2
blocks.body: Show that no bound $N(\sigma,T)\ll T^{A(1-\sigma)}(\log T)^B$ valid uniformly on $\tfrac12\le\sigma\le1$ can have $A<2$, and that $A=2$ forces $B\ge1$.
blocks.solution: Put $\sigma=\tfrac12$. By the symmetry $\rho\mapsto1-\bar\rho$, at least half of the zeros with $0<\gamma\le T$ have $\beta\ge\tfrac12$, so $N(\tfrac12,T)\ge\tfrac12N(T)\ge cT\log T$ for large $T$. The bound would give $cT\log T\ll T^{A/2}(\log T)^B$. If $A<2$, the right side is $o(T)$, a contradiction. If $A=2$, it reads $T\log T\ll T(\log T)^B$, which needs $B\ge1$.

blocks.title: Example 3: when does the first density bound say something?
blocks.body: Take $\sigma=\tfrac34$ in the clean form of the first density bound, ignoring the $o(1)$. Compare $N(\tfrac34,T)\lesssim cT$, with $c=\frac{\log\zeta(5/4)}{2\pi\cdot(1/4)}$, against the trivial bound $N(\tfrac34,T)\le\tfrac12N(T)$, where $N(T)\approx\frac{T}{2\pi}\log\frac{T}{2\pi e}$. Roughly from what height on is the density bound better?
blocks.solution:
We have $\zeta(1.25)\approx4.595$, so $c=\log(4.595)/(\pi/2)\approx1.525/1.571\approx0.971$. The density bound wins when $0.971\,T<\frac{T}{4\pi}\log\frac{T}{2\pi e}$, i.e. $\log\frac{T}{2\pi e}>4\pi\cdot0.971\approx12.2$, i.e. $T$ larger than about $3\times10^6$.

The lesson: a bound $O(T)$ against $N(T)\asymp T\log T$ saves only a logarithm, and logarithms grow slowly. The power-saving theorems save powers of $T$, which is why they, and not this one, are used for primes.

blocks.title: Example 4: the coefficients of ζ times a mollifier
blocks.body:
Let $X\ge1$ and $a_n=\sum_{d\mid n,\ d\le X}\mu(d)$. Show that $a_1=1$, that $a_n=0$ for $2\le n\le X$, and that $|a_n|\le\tau(n)$ for all $n$. Deduce that for $\mathrm{Re}\,s>1$
$$\zeta(s)\sum_{d\le X}\frac{\mu(d)}{d^s}=1+\sum_{n>X}\frac{a_n}{n^s}.$$
blocks.solution:
If $n\le X$, every divisor of $n$ is at most $X$, so $a_n=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)$, which is $1$ for $n=1$ and $0$ for $n>1$ (the basic property of the Möbius function, [[mobius]]). In general $a_n$ is a sum of at most $\tau(n)$ terms each equal to $0$ or $\pm1$, so $|a_n|\le\tau(n)$.

For $\mathrm{Re}\,s>1$ both series converge absolutely, so we may multiply and collect terms with $dm=n$:
$$\zeta(s)\sum_{d\le X}\mu(d)d^{-s}=\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-s}\sum_{d\mid n,\ d\le X}\mu(d)=\sum_n a_nn^{-s},$$
and the terms with $n\le X$ reduce to the single term $1$.

For example with $X=6$: $a_7=\mu(1)=1$, $a_8=\mu(1)+\mu(2)=0$, $a_{12}=\mu(1)+\mu(2)+\mu(3)+\mu(6)=0$, $a_{30}=\mu(1)+\mu(2)+\mu(3)+\mu(5)+\mu(6)=1-1-1-1+1=-1$.

blocks.body:
- A density estimate is not a zero-free region. It allows zeros arbitrarily far to the right of $\tfrac12$ (but not past the zero-free region); it only limits their number. The two kinds of result are used together.
- $T^{A(1-\sigma)}$ is not small near $\sigma=\tfrac12$: there it is at least $T$. Density theorems are informative mainly for $\sigma$ well to the right of $\tfrac12$.
- The placement of $\varepsilon$ matters. $T^{A(1-\sigma)+\varepsilon}$ and $T^{(A+\varepsilon)(1-\sigma)}$ differ exactly near $\sigma=1$, the range that matters most for primes.

Density estimates sit between [[zero-free-region|zero-free regions]], which control $\sigma$ extremely close to $1$, and the full [[rh|Riemann hypothesis]]. Their inputs are mean values of $\zeta$ and of Dirichlet polynomials ([[moments]], [[large-sieve]]); bounds for $\zeta$ on the critical line feed in through Ingham's method, so progress on the [[lindelof|Lindelöf hypothesis]] improves density exponents. The outputs are results on primes in short intervals and gaps between primes ([[prime-patterns]]). For Dirichlet [[l-functions]], density estimates in the modulus aspect, often proved with the large sieve, are a key ingredient of the [[bombieri-vinogradov|Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem]] and of Linnik's theorem on the least prime in an arithmetic progression, where they are combined with the repulsion of [[siegel-zeros|exceptional zeros]].

1. Show that Carlson's exponent $4\sigma(1-\sigma)$ is larger than Ingham's $3(1-\sigma)/(2-\sigma)$ for every $\sigma\in(\tfrac12,1)$, so Carlson's bound is always the weaker one.
2. Deduce from the first density bound that for each fixed $\delta>0$ the proportion of zeros with $0<\gamma\le T$ and $|\beta-\tfrac12|>\delta$ tends to $0$ as $T\to\infty$.
3. In the proof of the first density bound, replace the mean value theorem by the pointwise bound $|\zeta(\sigma_0+it)|\ll|t|^{1/2}$. What bound for $N(\sigma,T)$ do you get, and why is it useless?
4. Following the short-interval argument, find the exponent $\theta$ that a hypothetical bound $N(\sigma,T)\ll T^{\frac{5}{2}(1-\sigma)}(\log T)^{10}$ would give.

blocks.body:
How large can $|\zeta(\tfrac12+it)|$ get as $t\to\infty$? To the right of the line $\mathrm{Re}\,s=1$ the zeta function is bounded; to the left of $\mathrm{Re}\,s=0$ the functional equation makes it grow like a power of $|t|$. The critical line sits in between, and the size of $\zeta$ there governs moments, zero counts and primes in short intervals.

In 1908 Ernst Lindelöf conjectured that on the critical line $\zeta$ grows more slowly than any power of $t$. This is still open. What can be proved for free is the exponent $\tfrac14$; every improvement on it is called a subconvexity bound, and the same name is used for the analogous problem for every $L$-function.

blocks.title: The Lindelöf function and the Lindelöf hypothesis
blocks.body:
For real $\sigma$ let
$$\mu(\sigma)=\inf\{a\in\mathbb R:\ \zeta(\sigma+it)\ll|t|^{a}\ \text{as }|t|\to\infty\}.$$
The Lindelöf hypothesis (LH) is the statement $\mu(\tfrac12)=0$, that is,
$$\zeta(\tfrac12+it)\ll_\varepsilon|t|^{\varepsilon}\qquad\text{for every }\varepsilon>0.$$
So $\mu(\sigma)$ is the growth exponent of $\zeta$ on the vertical line $\mathrm{Re}\,s=\sigma$, and LH says that on the critical line there is no power growth at all.

blocks.title: What is known for free
blocks.body:
For $\sigma>1$, $|\zeta(\sigma+it)|\le\zeta(\sigma)$, so $\mu(\sigma)=0$. On the line $\sigma=1$ one has $\zeta(1+it)\ll\log|t|$, so $\mu(1)=0$ as well.

The [[functional-equation|functional equation]] $\zeta(s)=\chi(s)\zeta(1-s)$, with
$$\chi(s)=2^{s}\pi^{s-1}\sin\Bigl(\frac{\pi s}{2}\Bigr)\Gamma(1-s),$$
transfers information from the right to the left. Stirling's formula gives
$$|\chi(\sigma+it)|=\Bigl(\frac{|t|}{2\pi}\Bigr)^{1/2-\sigma}\bigl(1+O(1/|t|)\bigr)$$
uniformly for $\sigma$ in a bounded interval. In particular $|\chi(\tfrac12+it)|=1$ exactly (this follows from $\chi(s)\chi(1-s)=1$ and $\overline{\chi(s)}=\chi(\bar s)$), and taking growth exponents in the functional equation gives
$$\mu(\sigma)=\tfrac12-\sigma+\mu(1-\sigma).$$
For $\sigma\le0$ this yields $\mu(\sigma)=\tfrac12-\sigma$ exactly. So we know $\mu$ on both sides of the critical strip; the whole problem is the strip $0<\sigma<1$.

blocks.title: Convexity bound
blocks.body:
The function $\mu$ is convex, continuous and non-increasing on $\mathbb R$, and
$$\mu(\sigma)\le\frac{1-\sigma}{2}\quad(0\le\sigma\le1),\qquad\text{in particular}\qquad\zeta(\tfrac12+it)\ll_\varepsilon|t|^{1/4+\varepsilon}.$$

blocks.title: Proof of the convexity bound
blocks.body:
The tool is the Phragmén–Lindelöf principle, a maximum principle for vertical strips: if $f$ is holomorphic on $a\le\mathrm{Re}\,s\le b$, satisfies a crude growth bound such as $|f(s)|\ll e^{|t|^{C}}$ there, and $|f(a+it)|\ll(1+|t|)^{\alpha}$, $|f(b+it)|\ll(1+|t|)^{\beta}$, then
$$|f(\sigma+it)|\ll(1+|t|)^{\ell(\sigma)},\qquad \ell(\sigma)=\alpha\,\frac{b-\sigma}{b-a}+\beta\,\frac{\sigma-a}{b-a},$$
for $a\le\sigma\le b$. Applying this on every strip shows that $\mu$ is convex: its graph lies below each chord. (Apply it to $(s-1)\zeta(s)$, which is entire; the factor $s-1$ adds $1$ to the exponent on both edges and therefore to $\ell$, and is then removed.) A convex function that vanishes on $[1,\infty)$ cannot increase anywhere, otherwise it would tend to $+\infty$ to the right; so $\mu$ is non-increasing, and a finite convex function is continuous.

Now take $\delta>0$ and the strip $-\delta\le\sigma\le1+\delta$. On the right edge $|\zeta|\le\zeta(1+\delta)$, exponent $\beta=0$. On the left edge $|\zeta(-\delta+it)|=|\chi(-\delta+it)|\,|\zeta(1+\delta-it)|\ll|t|^{1/2+\delta}$, exponent $\alpha=\tfrac12+\delta$. At $\sigma=\tfrac12$,
$$\ell(\tfrac12)=\Bigl(\tfrac12+\delta\Bigr)\frac{(1+\delta)-\tfrac12}{1+2\delta}=\frac{(\tfrac12+\delta)^2}{1+2\delta}=\frac14+\frac\delta2.$$
Taking $\delta=2\varepsilon$ gives $\zeta(\tfrac12+it)\ll|t|^{1/4+\varepsilon}$. The same interpolation between $\mu(0)=\tfrac12$ and $\mu(1)=0$ gives $\mu(\sigma)\le\frac{1-\sigma}{2}$ on $[0,1]$.

blocks.title: Why 1/4 is the trivial bound and LH is cancellation
blocks.body:
The convexity bound has a transparent meaning. The Riemann–Siegel form of the approximate functional equation says that for large $t$, with $N=\lfloor\sqrt{t/2\pi}\rfloor$,
$$\zeta(\tfrac12+it)=\sum_{n\le N}n^{-1/2-it}+\chi(\tfrac12+it)\sum_{n\le N}n^{-1/2+it}+O(t^{-1/4}).$$
Both sums have length about $\sqrt t$, and $|\chi(\tfrac12+it)|=1$. Bounding every term by its absolute value gives at most $2\sum_{n\le N}n^{-1/2}<4\sqrt N\approx4(t/2\pi)^{1/4}$ (Example 1). So convexity is what you get by assuming no cancellation at all among the phases $t\log n$.

If the terms $n^{-it}$ behaved like independent random unit vectors, a sum of $M$ of them would typically have size about $\sqrt M$. A bound of the form $\bigl|\sum_{n\le M}n^{-it}\bigr|\ll M^{1/2}t^{\varepsilon}$ for all $M\le\sqrt t$ would, after partial summation, give LH. Thus LH is a square-root cancellation statement for the exponential sums $\sum n^{-it}=\sum e^{-it\log n}$, and the attack on it is the theory of [[exponential-sums|exponential sums]]: Weyl differencing and van der Corput's method replace the sum by sums with smoother phases, and each step saves a power of $t$.

blocks.title: History of the exponent
blocks.body:
Writing $\zeta(\tfrac12+it)\ll|t|^{c+\varepsilon}$:
- $c=\tfrac14=0.25$: convexity.
- $c=\tfrac16\approx0.1667$: Hardy and Littlewood, using Weyl's differencing method (around 1920). The exponent $\tfrac16$ is often called the Weyl exponent, and Weyl-strength bounds are a benchmark for every $L$-function.
- $c=\tfrac{9}{56}\approx0.1607$: Bombieri and Iwaniec (1986), a new method for exponential sums.
- $c=\tfrac{32}{205}\approx0.1561$: Huxley (2005), refining Bombieri–Iwaniec.
- $c=\tfrac{13}{84}\approx0.1548$: Bourgain (2017), combining the Bombieri–Iwaniec method with decoupling estimates from harmonic analysis.

Many intermediate improvements, by van der Corput, Titchmarsh, Kolesnik and others, are omitted. The progress since 1920 is less than $0.012$ in the exponent, which gives a sense of how hard the problem is.

blocks.title: Equivalent forms and consequences
blocks.body:
1. (Hardy and Littlewood) LH holds if and only if for every integer $k\ge1$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, $\displaystyle\int_0^T|\zeta(\tfrac12+it)|^{2k}dt\ll T^{1+\varepsilon}$.
2. (Backlund) LH holds if and only if for every $\sigma>\tfrac12$ the number of zeros with $\beta\ge\sigma$ and $T\le\gamma\le T+1$ is $o(\log T)$. For comparison, the total number of zeros with $T\le\gamma\le T+1$ is $O(\log T)$, and about $\frac{1}{2\pi}\log T$ on average.
3. (Littlewood) The Riemann hypothesis implies LH, and in fact gives $\zeta(\tfrac12+it)\ll\exp\bigl(C\log t/\log\log t\bigr)$ for some constant $C$.
4. (Ingham) If $\zeta(\tfrac12+it)\ll t^{c}$, then $N(\sigma,T)\ll T^{(2+4c)(1-\sigma)}(\log T)^5$. In particular LH implies the density hypothesis of [[zero-density]], and hence $p_{n+1}-p_n\ll p_n^{1/2+\varepsilon}$.

blocks.title: Subconvexity for other L-functions
blocks.body:
Every $L$-function with a functional equation has a convexity bound obtained exactly as above. For a Dirichlet $L$-function with primitive character $\chi$ modulo $q$, the functional equation relates $L(s,\chi)$ to $L(1-s,\bar\chi)$ with a factor of size about $(q(|t|+1))^{1/2-\sigma}$, and Phragmén–Lindelöf gives $L(\tfrac12,\chi)\ll_\varepsilon q^{1/4+\varepsilon}$. A subconvexity bound is any bound $q^{1/4-\delta}$ with fixed $\delta>0$. Known landmarks:
- Burgess (1962–63): $L(\tfrac12,\chi)\ll_\varepsilon q^{3/16+\varepsilon}$, from his bound for short character sums.
- Conrey and Iwaniec (2000): $q^{1/6+\varepsilon}$ for quadratic characters, the Weyl exponent in the $q$-aspect.
- Michel and Venkatesh (2010): subconvexity for all $\mathrm{GL}(2)$ $L$-functions, in every aspect at once.

Subconvexity is often exactly what an application needs: a power saving over the trivial bound, however small. Several equidistribution theorems (for example of lattice points on spheres or of special points on modular curves) are proved by reducing them to subconvex bounds for suitable $L$-values.

blocks.title: Example 1: the trivial bound for the approximate functional equation
blocks.body:
Prove that for every integer $N\ge2$
$$2\sqrt{N+1}-2<\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac1{\sqrt n}<2\sqrt N-1,$$
and deduce that the two main sums in the approximate functional equation have total absolute value less than $4(t/2\pi)^{1/4}$.
blocks.solution:
For $n\ge1$,
$$\sqrt{n+1}-\sqrt n=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n+1}+\sqrt n}<\frac1{2\sqrt n}<\frac{1}{\sqrt n+\sqrt{n-1}}=\sqrt n-\sqrt{n-1}.$$
Summing the left inequality over $1\le n\le N$ telescopes to $\sqrt{N+1}-1<\tfrac12\sum_{n\le N}n^{-1/2}$. Summing the right inequality over $2\le n\le N$ gives $\tfrac12\sum_{2\le n\le N}n^{-1/2}<\sqrt N-1$, so $\sum_{n\le N}n^{-1/2}<1+2\sqrt N-2=2\sqrt N-1$.

With $N=\lfloor\sqrt{t/2\pi}\rfloor$ each main sum is at most $\sum_{n\le N}n^{-1/2}<2\sqrt N\le2(t/2\pi)^{1/4}$, and $|\chi(\tfrac12+it)|=1$, so together they are less than $4(t/2\pi)^{1/4}$. For $N=10$ the sum is $5.021$, between $4.633$ and $5.325$; for $N=100$ it is $18.590$, between $18.100$ and $19$.

blocks.title: Example 2: LH pins down the whole function μ
blocks.body: Show that LH is equivalent to $\mu(\sigma)=\max(0,\tfrac12-\sigma)$ for all real $\sigma$. You may use that $\mu(\sigma)\ge0$ for $\sigma\ge\tfrac12$, which follows from mean values: $\frac1T\int_1^T|\zeta(\sigma+it)|^2dt$ tends to $\zeta(2\sigma)$ for $\sigma>\tfrac12$ and grows like $\log T$ for $\sigma=\tfrac12$, which would be impossible if $|\zeta(\sigma+it)|\ll|t|^{-a}$ with $a>0$.
blocks.solution:
If $\mu(\sigma)=\max(0,\tfrac12-\sigma)$ everywhere then $\mu(\tfrac12)=0$, which is LH.

Conversely assume $\mu(\tfrac12)=0$. For $\sigma\ge\tfrac12$, since $\mu$ is non-increasing and $\mu\ge0$ there, $0\le\mu(\sigma)\le\mu(\tfrac12)=0$. For $\sigma<\tfrac12$ we have $1-\sigma>\tfrac12$, so $\mu(1-\sigma)=0$ and the relation $\mu(\sigma)=\tfrac12-\sigma+\mu(1-\sigma)$ gives $\mu(\sigma)=\tfrac12-\sigma$.

So under LH the graph of $\mu$ is the broken line made of $\tfrac12-\sigma$ on the left and $0$ on the right, meeting at the critical line, while convexity only guarantees the chord from $(0,\tfrac12)$ to $(1,0)$ as an upper bound. The convexity bound is the straight line; LH is the corner.

blocks.title: Example 3: numbers at modest height
blocks.body: At $t=1000$ compare $\zeta(\tfrac12+it)$ with the two main sums of the approximate functional equation ($N=12$). Then look at the size of $|\zeta(\tfrac12+it)|$ for $t\le1000$ and compare it with $t^{1/4}$.
blocks.solution:
Numerically, $|\zeta(\tfrac12+1000i)|\approx0.998$, and the main sums with $N=12$ reproduce it with an error of about $0.114$, compared with $t^{-1/4}\approx0.178$. At $t=10^4$ ($N=39$) the error is about $0.111$ against $t^{-1/4}=0.1$. So the error really is of order $t^{-1/4}$ and the approximation is excellent.

On the other hand $|\zeta(\tfrac12+it)|$ exceeds $9.4$ near $t\approx897.85$, while $897.85^{1/4}\approx5.47$. This does not contradict anything: $\ll$ hides constants, and at such heights $\log t$ factors are as large as small powers of $t$. The Lindelöf hypothesis and its relatives are statements about growth rates and cannot be tested by looking at values at moderate height.

blocks.title: Example 4: from bounds on ζ to density exponents and prime gaps
blocks.body: Using item 4 of the theorem on equivalent forms together with the theorem on primes in short intervals from [[zero-density]] (density exponent $A$ gives intervals $x^{\theta}$ for every $\theta>1-1/A$), compute $A$ and $\theta$ for $c=\tfrac14,\ \tfrac16,\ \tfrac{13}{84}$ and for LH ($c\to0$).
blocks.solution:
Ingham's bound has $A=2+4c$.
- $c=\tfrac14$: $A=3$, $\theta>\tfrac23$.
- $c=\tfrac16$: $A=\tfrac83$, $\theta>1-\tfrac38=\tfrac58$. This is Ingham's 1937 theorem $p_{n+1}-p_n\ll p_n^{5/8+\varepsilon}$.
- $c=\tfrac{13}{84}$: $A=2+\tfrac{52}{84}=\tfrac{55}{21}$, $\theta>1-\tfrac{21}{55}=\tfrac{34}{55}\approx0.618$.
- LH: $A=2+\varepsilon$, every $\theta>\tfrac12$.

Note that Huxley's density exponent $\tfrac{12}{5}=2.4$ is better than $\tfrac{55}{21}\approx2.619$: density estimates improve not only through bounds for $\zeta$ but also through better large values estimates for Dirichlet polynomials.

blocks.body:
- LH is not RH. It is a statement about size; it is compatible with zeros off the critical line, provided they are sparse in the sense of Backlund's criterion.
- $\zeta(\tfrac12+it)$ is unbounded. LH asserts growth slower than every power of $t$, not boundedness.
- The exponents in the history list are infima: a bound $\ll t^{13/84+\varepsilon}$ for every $\varepsilon$ is what is proved, not $\ll t^{13/84}$.
- Convexity needs a functional equation and polynomial growth on the edges. An arbitrary Dirichlet series has no such bound for free.
- Numerical values at moderate height say nothing about these exponents (Example 3).

The convexity bound is a direct consequence of the [[functional-equation]], and all subconvexity results for $\zeta$ come from estimates for [[exponential-sums]]. LH is equivalent to bounds for all [[moments]] of $\zeta$, implies the density hypothesis ([[zero-density]]) and so gives good results on primes in short intervals ([[prime-patterns]]). It is itself a consequence of the [[rh|Riemann hypothesis]], and the [[grh|generalized Riemann hypothesis]] likewise implies a generalized Lindelöf hypothesis for [[l-functions]], whose subconvexity problem is a central theme of modern analytic number theory.

1. Use the functional equation to show that $\mu(-1)=\tfrac32$ and more generally $\mu(\sigma)=\tfrac12-\sigma$ for $\sigma\le0$.
2. Show that LH implies $\int_0^T|\zeta(\tfrac12+it)|^{2k}dt\ll_{k,\varepsilon}T^{1+\varepsilon}$ for every $k$ (the easy direction of the Hardy–Littlewood equivalence).
3. Assuming the approximate functional equation, show that a bound $\bigl|\sum_{n\le M}n^{-it}\bigr|\ll M^{1/2}t^{\varepsilon}$ for all $M\le\sqrt{t/2\pi}$ would imply $\zeta(\tfrac12+it)\ll t^{2\varepsilon}$. (Use partial summation.)
4. Show that $\chi(s)\chi(1-s)=1$ and deduce that $|\chi(\tfrac12+it)|=1$ for real $t$.

blocks.body:
The nontrivial zeros of $\zeta$ up to height $T$ number about $\frac{T}{2\pi}\log\frac{T}{2\pi}$, so near height $T$ consecutive ordinates are on average $2\pi/\log\frac{T}{2\pi}$ apart. That is a statement about the average spacing. The finer question is what the spacings look like: are the zeros scattered like independent random points, arranged like a lattice, or something in between?

In 1973 Hugh Montgomery proved a partial answer, assuming the Riemann hypothesis, and conjectured the full one: zeros repel each other, and the density of pairs at normalised distance $u$ is $1-\bigl(\frac{\sin\pi u}{\pi u}\bigr)^2$. Freeman Dyson recognised this function at once: it is the pair correlation of eigenvalues of large random Hermitian matrices. This coincidence has since grown into a programme that predicts many statistics of zeta and $L$-functions.

blocks.title: Unfolding: measuring gaps in the right units
blocks.body:
Throughout, assume RH, so the nontrivial zeros are $\tfrac12+i\gamma$ with real $\gamma$. By the Riemann–von Mangoldt formula ([[nontrivial-zeros]]) the number of zeros with $0<\gamma\le T$ is $N(T)=\frac{T}{2\pi}\log\frac{T}{2\pi e}+O(\log T)$, so the local density of zeros near height $t$ is $\frac1{2\pi}\log\frac{t}{2\pi}$ and slowly increases.

To compare spacings at different heights we rescale so that the mean spacing is $1$. One convenient way: replace each $\gamma$ by $\tilde\gamma=\frac{\vartheta(\gamma)}{\pi}+1$, where $\vartheta(t)=\frac t2\log\frac t{2\pi}-\frac t2-\frac\pi8+O(1/t)$ is the Riemann–Siegel theta function; this is the smooth part of $N(t)$. Then consecutive $\tilde\gamma$ differ by $1$ on average. Montgomery used the simpler scaling by $\frac{\log T}{2\pi}$ for all zeros up to height $T$, which is the same to first order.

After unfolding, independent random points (a Poisson process of rate $1$) would have gaps with density $e^{-s}$, so many very small gaps: a fraction $1-e^{-0.2}\approx0.18$ of them below $0.2$. A lattice would have all gaps equal to $1$. The zeros do neither.

blocks.title: Pair correlation of the zeros
blocks.body:
For $0<a<b$ let
$$R_T(a,b)=\#\Bigl\{(\gamma,\gamma'):\ 0<\gamma,\gamma'\le T,\ \gamma\ne\gamma',\ a\le(\gamma-\gamma')\frac{\log T}{2\pi}\le b\Bigr\}.$$
A function $g$ is the pair correlation density of the zeros if $R_T(a,b)\sim N(T)\int_a^bg(u)\,du$ for all such $a,b$.

In words, $\int_a^bg$ is the expected number of other zeros lying at normalised distance between $a$ and $b$ above a typical zero. For a Poisson process $g\equiv1$.

blocks.title: Montgomery's theorem (assuming RH)
blocks.body:
Let $w(u)=\frac{4}{4+u^2}$ and for real $\alpha$ and $T\ge2$ define
$$F(\alpha)=F(\alpha,T)=\frac{2\pi}{T\log T}\sum_{0<\gamma,\gamma'\le T}T^{i\alpha(\gamma-\gamma')}\,w(\gamma-\gamma').$$
Then $F$ is real, even and non-negative, and as $T\to\infty$
$$F(\alpha)=(1+o(1))\,T^{-2|\alpha|}\log T+|\alpha|+o(1)$$
uniformly for $|\alpha|\le1$. (Montgomery proved this for $|\alpha|\le1-\varepsilon$; the extension to the endpoint $|\alpha|=1$ uses a later refinement of Goldston and Montgomery.)

blocks.title: Montgomery's pair correlation conjecture
blocks.body:
Conjecture: $F(\alpha)=1+o(1)$ uniformly for $\alpha$ in any bounded set with $|\alpha|\ge1$. Together with Montgomery's theorem this would imply that the pair correlation density of the zeros is
$$g(u)=1-\Bigl(\frac{\sin\pi u}{\pi u}\Bigr)^2.$$

blocks.title: From F(α) to the function 1 − (sin πu/πu)²
blocks.body:
Why does $F$ encode pair correlation? Take a nice even test function $r$ with Fourier transform $\hat r(\alpha)=\int r(u)e^{-2\pi i\alpha u}du$. Writing $r(u)=\int\hat r(\alpha)e^{2\pi i\alpha u}d\alpha$ and noting $e^{2\pi i\alpha(\gamma-\gamma')\log T/2\pi}=T^{i\alpha(\gamma-\gamma')}$,
$$\sum_{0<\gamma,\gamma'\le T}r\Bigl((\gamma-\gamma')\frac{\log T}{2\pi}\Bigr)w(\gamma-\gamma')=\frac{T\log T}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}F(\alpha)\hat r(\alpha)\,d\alpha.$$
So knowing $F$ is the same as knowing all such weighted pair sums. The weight $w(\gamma-\gamma')$ is harmless: on the scale of the mean spacing, which tends to $0$, it is essentially $w(0)=1$.

Now suppose $F(\alpha)\approx1-\max(1-|\alpha|,0)+T^{-2|\alpha|}\log T$ for all $\alpha$, which is what the theorem and the conjecture say together. Integrate term by term against $\hat r$:
- $\int\hat r(\alpha)\,d\alpha=r(0)$;
- $\int\max(1-|\alpha|,0)\hat r(\alpha)\,d\alpha=\int r(u)\bigl(\frac{\sin\pi u}{\pi u}\bigr)^2du$, by the Fourier pair proved below;
- the spike $T^{-2|\alpha|}\log T$ has total integral $1$ and concentrates at $\alpha=0$, so it contributes $\hat r(0)=\int r(u)\,du$.
Altogether
$$\sum_{0<\gamma,\gamma'\le T}r\Bigl((\gamma-\gamma')\tfrac{\log T}{2\pi}\Bigr)w(\gamma-\gamma')\approx N(T)\Bigl(r(0)+\int_{-\infty}^\infty r(u)\Bigl(1-\Bigl(\frac{\sin\pi u}{\pi u}\Bigr)^2\Bigr)du\Bigr).$$
The term $r(0)N(T)$ is the diagonal $\gamma=\gamma'$; what remains says that pairs of distinct zeros have density $1-(\sin\pi u/\pi u)^2$. Montgomery's theorem proves this for test functions with $\hat r$ supported in $[-1,1]$; the conjecture is needed for all others.

blocks.title: A Fourier pair
blocks.body:
For every real $u$,
$$\int_{-1}^{1}(1-|\alpha|)\,e^{2\pi i\alpha u}\,d\alpha=\Bigl(\frac{\sin\pi u}{\pi u}\Bigr)^2,$$
(with value $1$ at $u=0$), and consequently $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\bigl(\frac{\sin\pi u}{\pi u}\bigr)^2e^{-2\pi i\alpha u}du=\max(1-|\alpha|,0)$; in particular $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\bigl(\frac{\sin\pi u}{\pi u}\bigr)^2du=1$.

Let $I$ be the indicator function of $[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]$. Its Fourier integral is
$$\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}e^{2\pi ixu}dx=\frac{e^{\pi iu}-e^{-\pi iu}}{2\pi iu}=\frac{\sin\pi u}{\pi u}.$$
The convolution $(I*I)(\alpha)=\int I(x)I(\alpha-x)\,dx$ is the length of $[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]\cap[\alpha-\tfrac12,\alpha+\tfrac12]$, which is $\max(1-|\alpha|,0)$. By Fubini and the substitution $\alpha=x+y$,
$$\int(I*I)(\alpha)e^{2\pi i\alpha u}d\alpha=\int\!\!\int I(x)I(y)e^{2\pi i(x+y)u}\,dx\,dy=\Bigl(\frac{\sin\pi u}{\pi u}\Bigr)^2.$$
This is the first claim. The triangle function is continuous and integrable, and so is its transform $(\sin\pi u/\pi u)^2$, so the Fourier inversion theorem ([[fourier-poisson]]) applies and gives the second claim; put $\alpha=0$ for the third.

blocks.title: What random matrices have to do with it
blocks.body:
The Gaussian Unitary Ensemble (GUE) is the probability distribution on $n\times n$ Hermitian matrices with density proportional to $e^{-\mathrm{tr}(H^2)}$; it is invariant under conjugation by unitary matrices. Its eigenvalues $x_1,\dots,x_n$ are real ([[spectral-theorem]]) and have joint density proportional to
$$\prod_{j<k}(x_j-x_k)^2\,e^{-\sum_jx_j^2}.$$
The squared Vandermonde factor makes nearby eigenvalues unlikely: the probability of two eigenvalues within $\varepsilon$ of each other is of order $\varepsilon^3$ rather than $\varepsilon$. After unfolding to mean spacing $1$, as $n\to\infty$ the pair correlation of the eigenvalues tends to exactly $1-(\sin\pi u/\pi u)^2$ (Dyson; Gaudin and Mehta). The same local statistics hold for the eigenvalue angles of a random unitary matrix chosen with Haar measure (the circular unitary ensemble, CUE), which is the model most often used for $\zeta$.

Near $u=0$ the function behaves like $\frac{\pi^2u^2}{3}$, quadratic vanishing that expresses repulsion. For large $u$ it tends to $1$: zeros far apart are uncorrelated.

Physicists had met GUE statistics as the energy levels of quantum systems whose classical dynamics is chaotic and not time-reversal symmetric. This fits the Hilbert–Pólya idea that the $\gamma$ might be the eigenvalues of some self-adjoint operator, which would prove RH. No such operator is known.

blocks.title: Evidence and consequences
blocks.body:
- Numerics. Andrew Odlyzko (from 1987 onward) computed large batches of zeros at great heights, including near the $10^{20}$-th zero. Their spacing histograms and pair correlation match the GUE predictions remarkably well. Example 2 below is a tiny version of this experiment.
- Simple zeros. From his theorem Montgomery deduced, assuming RH, that at least two thirds of the zeros are simple (Example 3).
- Higher correlations. Rudnick and Sarnak (1996) proved that the $n$-level correlations of zeros agree with GUE for test functions whose Fourier transforms have restricted support, extending Montgomery's theorem.
- Primes. Goldston and Montgomery showed, assuming RH, that the pair correlation conjecture is equivalent to an asymptotic formula for the variance of the number of primes in short intervals. So the conjecture is really a statement about pairs of primes, in the spirit of the Hardy–Littlewood prime-tuple conjectures.
- Moments. Keating and Snaith (2000) used the CUE to predict the moments of $\zeta$ on the critical line ([[moments]]):
$$\frac1T\int_0^T|\zeta(\tfrac12+it)|^{2k}dt\sim a_k\,\frac{G(k+1)^2}{G(2k+1)}\,(\log T)^{k^2},\qquad a_k=\prod_p\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr)^{k^2}\sum_{m\ge0}\binom{m+k-1}{k-1}^2p^{-m},$$
where $G$ is the Barnes $G$-function ($G(1)=1$, $G(z+1)=\Gamma(z)G(z)$). The random matrix factor $G(k+1)^2/G(2k+1)$ times $(k^2)!$ equals $1,2,42,24024$ for $k=1,2,3,4$: the first two agree with the theorems of Hardy–Littlewood and Ingham, and the last two with earlier predictions of Conrey–Ghosh and Conrey–Gonek made by number-theoretic heuristics.
- Families. Katz and Sarnak found that zeros near the central point, averaged over a family of $L$-functions, should follow the statistics of one of the classical groups (unitary, symplectic or orthogonal), according to the symmetry of the family; this has been proved in many families for test functions of restricted support.

blocks.title: Example 1: how strong is the repulsion?
blocks.body: Prove that $1-\bigl(\frac{\sin x}{x}\bigr)^2\le\frac{x^2}{3}$ for all real $x\ne0$. Deduce that, if the pair correlation conjecture holds, the expected number of zeros within normalised distance $\varepsilon$ above a typical zero is at most $\pi^2\varepsilon^3/9$, compared with $\varepsilon$ for independent points.
blocks.solution:
By symmetry take $x>0$. If $x^2\ge3$ the right side is at least $1$ while the left side is at most $1$, so there is nothing to prove. If $0<x<\sqrt3$, use $\sin x\ge x-\frac{x^3}{6}$ for $x\ge0$ (integrate $\cos y\ge1-y^2/2$ from $0$ to $x$, which in turn comes from integrating $\sin y\le y$). Here $x-\frac{x^3}{6}>0$, so
$$\sin^2x\ge\Bigl(x-\frac{x^3}6\Bigr)^2=x^2-\frac{x^4}{3}+\frac{x^6}{36}\ge x^2-\frac{x^4}{3}.$$
Dividing by $x^2$ gives the claim.

With $x=\pi u$: $g(u)=1-\bigl(\frac{\sin\pi u}{\pi u}\bigr)^2\le\frac{\pi^2u^2}{3}$, so $\int_0^\varepsilon g\le\frac{\pi^2\varepsilon^3}{9}$. For $\varepsilon=0.1$ this is about $0.0011$, against $0.1$ for a Poisson process: close pairs are about a hundred times rarer.

blocks.title: Example 2: a small experiment
blocks.body: Compute the $649$ zeros with $0<\gamma\le1000$, unfold them by $\tilde\gamma=\vartheta(\gamma)/\pi+1$, and compare (a) the smallest gaps with the Poisson prediction and (b) the average number of later zeros within unfolded distance $1$ with $\int_0^1\bigl(1-(\frac{\sin\pi u}{\pi u})^2\bigr)du$.
blocks.solution:
Sign changes of the Riemann–Siegel function $Z(t)$ on a grid of step $0.1$, refined by root finding, locate $649$ zeros, which matches the exact count $N(1000)=649$, so none was missed. After unfolding, the mean gap is $1.00$.

(a) Not a single unfolded gap is below $0.2$; for independent points about $18\%$ would be.

(b) On average a zero has $0.547$ later zeros within distance $1$. The prediction is $\int_0^1(1-(\frac{\sin\pi u}{\pi u})^2)du\approx0.549$; independent points would give $1$.

The agreement in (b) is better than one should expect from so few low zeros, and at this height there are known small deviations from the limiting GUE statistics; but the repulsion in (a) is unmistakable.

blocks.title: Example 3: at least two thirds of the zeros are simple
blocks.body:
Assume RH and Montgomery's theorem. Use the test function $r(u)=\bigl(\frac{\sin\pi u}{\pi u}\bigr)^2$ to show that
$$\sum_{0<\gamma\le T}m_\gamma\le\Bigl(\frac43+o(1)\Bigr)N(T),$$
where the sum runs over zeros counted with multiplicity and $m_\gamma$ is the multiplicity. Deduce that at least $(\tfrac23-o(1))N(T)$ of the zeros up to height $T$ are simple.
blocks.solution:
By the Fourier pair, $\hat r(\alpha)=\max(1-|\alpha|,0)$, supported in $[-1,1]$ where Montgomery's theorem applies. The identity for weighted pair sums gives
$$\sum_{\gamma,\gamma'}r\Bigl((\gamma-\gamma')\tfrac{\log T}{2\pi}\Bigr)w(\gamma-\gamma')=\frac{T\log T}{2\pi}\int_{-1}^1F(\alpha)(1-|\alpha|)\,d\alpha.$$
Insert $F(\alpha)=|\alpha|+(1+o(1))T^{-2|\alpha|}\log T+o(1)$. First, $\int_{-1}^1|\alpha|(1-|\alpha|)d\alpha=2(\tfrac12-\tfrac13)=\tfrac13$. Second, with $L=\log T$,
$$\int_{-1}^1T^{-2|\alpha|}L(1-|\alpha|)\,d\alpha=2L\int_0^1e^{-2L\alpha}(1-\alpha)\,d\alpha=1-\frac{1-e^{-2L}}{2L}\to1.$$
So the right side is $(\tfrac43+o(1))\frac{T\log T}{2\pi}=(\tfrac43+o(1))N(T)$.

On the left every term is non-negative, since $r\ge0$ and $w>0$. Keep only the pairs with $\gamma=\gamma'$, where $r(0)=w(0)=1$. In the double sum over zeros counted with multiplicity, a zero of multiplicity $m$ gives $m^2$ such pairs, and $\sum_{\text{distinct}}m^2=\sum_{\text{with mult.}}m_\gamma$. This proves the inequality.

Let $N_s$ be the number of simple zeros. Each multiple zero has $m^2\ge2m$, so
$$\sum_{\text{distinct}}m^2\ge N_s+2\bigl(N(T)-N_s\bigr)=2N(T)-N_s.$$
Combining, $2N(T)-N_s\le(\tfrac43+o(1))N(T)$, so $N_s\ge(\tfrac23-o(1))N(T)$.

blocks.title: Example 4: the random matrix prediction for the fourth moment
blocks.body: Check that the Keating–Snaith formula with $k=2$ reproduces Ingham's theorem $\frac1T\int_0^T|\zeta(\tfrac12+it)|^4dt\sim\frac{1}{2\pi^2}(\log T)^4$.
blocks.solution:
For $k=2$, $\binom{m+1}{1}^2=(m+1)^2$ and $\sum_{m\ge0}(m+1)^2x^m=\frac{1+x}{(1-x)^3}$. With $x=1/p$, the Euler factor is $(1-x)^4\frac{1+x}{(1-x)^3}=(1-x)(1+x)=1-p^{-2}$, so $a_2=\prod_p(1-p^{-2})=1/\zeta(2)=6/\pi^2$.

The random matrix factor is $G(3)^2/G(5)$. From $G(z+1)=\Gamma(z)G(z)$: $G(2)=G(3)=1$, $G(4)=2$, $G(5)=12$. So the constant is $\frac{6}{\pi^2}\cdot\frac{1}{12}=\frac{1}{2\pi^2}$, exactly Ingham's. For $k=1$ the same computation gives $a_1=1$ and factor $1$, which is the Hardy–Littlewood asymptotic $\frac1T\int_0^T|\zeta(\tfrac12+it)|^2dt\sim\log T$.

blocks.body:
- The pair correlation conjecture is not proved even under RH. Montgomery's theorem covers only $|\alpha|\le1$, that is, test functions with $\hat r$ supported in $[-1,1]$; detecting pairs at a specific distance needs all $\alpha$.
- Gaps must be measured after unfolding by the local density. Raw gaps mix heights where the density differs.
- The pair correlation function is not the distribution of nearest-neighbour gaps. Both are determined by GUE, but the gap distribution (the Gaudin distribution) is a different function.
- Agreement of statistics is evidence, not proof. Random matrix theory predicts the leading behaviour; arithmetic enters through factors such as $a_k$, which random matrices do not see.
- Low zeros show visible finite-height deviations; conclusions should not be drawn from a few hundred zeros.

Montgomery's theorem is proved from an explicit-formula-type identity linking sums over zeros to sums over primes ([[explicit-formula]]), so pair correlation is as much about primes as about zeros. The random matrix model ties the theory of [[nontrivial-zeros]] to the [[spectral-theorem]] and [[eigen|eigenvalues]] of large matrices, and to the [[rh|Riemann hypothesis]] through the Hilbert–Pólya idea. Its most quantitative successes are the moment conjectures ([[moments]]), and its extension to families of [[l-functions]] organises much of current work on low-lying zeros. The technique of the proof, integrating against a test function whose transform has limited support, is Fourier analysis ([[fourier-poisson]]).

1. Show that $w(u)=\frac4{4+u^2}$ equals $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-2|v|}e^{iuv}dv$, and use this to show $F(\alpha)\ge0$.
2. If the unfolded zeros were exactly the integers, what would the pair correlation "density" be? Contrast it with $1-(\sin\pi u/\pi u)^2$.
3. Assuming the conjecture, estimate the expected number of zeros within normalised distance $0.5$ above a typical zero, and compare with independent points.
4. Explain why the diagonal terms $\gamma=\gamma'$ contribute $r(0)N(T)$ to the weighted pair sum when all zeros are simple.

blocks.body:
Every real number can be approximated by fractions, since the rationals are dense. The interesting question is how well, measured against the size of the denominator. With denominator $q$ you can always get within $\frac1{2q}$ of $\alpha$, just by rounding $q\alpha$. Some numbers allow much better: $\frac{355}{113}$ is within $2.7\times10^{-7}$ of $\pi$, far closer than $\frac1{2\cdot113}$.

Diophantine approximation measures this by a power of $q$. It is a theory with two faces. A number that has extremely good rational approximations cannot be algebraic (Liouville, Roth). A number that has a sequence of good, but not perfect, approximations cannot be rational, which is how irrationality proofs such as Apéry's for $\zeta(3)$ work. And bounds on how well algebraic numbers can be approximated give finiteness theorems for Diophantine equations.

blocks.title: Irrationality exponent
blocks.body:
For real $\alpha$ the irrationality exponent $\mu(\alpha)$ is the supremum of all $\mu$ such that
$$0<\Bigl|\alpha-\frac pq\Bigr|<\frac{1}{q^{\mu}}$$
has infinitely many solutions in rationals $\frac pq$ with $q\ge1$.

It measures how fast the best approximations converge: rationals have $\mu=1$, every irrational has $\mu\ge2$ (Dirichlet, below), algebraic irrationals have $\mu=2$ exactly (Roth), and numbers with $\mu=\infty$ are called Liouville numbers.

blocks.title: Dirichlet's approximation theorem
blocks.body:
Let $\alpha$ be real and $N\ge1$ an integer. There are integers $p,q$ with $1\le q\le N$ and $|q\alpha-p|<\frac1N$. If $\alpha$ is irrational, there are infinitely many rationals $\frac pq$ with
$$\Bigl|\alpha-\frac pq\Bigr|<\frac{1}{q^2}.$$

Write $\{x\}=x-\lfloor x\rfloor$. The $N+1$ numbers $\{0\cdot\alpha\},\{1\cdot\alpha\},\dots,\{N\alpha\}$ lie in $[0,1)$, which is the union of the $N$ intervals $[\frac kN,\frac{k+1}N)$, $0\le k<N$. By the [[pigeonhole|pigeonhole principle]] two of them, say $\{i\alpha\}$ and $\{j\alpha\}$ with $0\le i<j\le N$, lie in the same interval, so $|\{j\alpha\}-\{i\alpha\}|<\frac1N$. With $q=j-i\in[1,N]$ and $p=\lfloor j\alpha\rfloor-\lfloor i\alpha\rfloor$ this says $|q\alpha-p|<\frac1N$. Dividing by $q$ and using $q\le N$: $|\alpha-\frac pq|<\frac1{qN}\le\frac1{q^2}$.

Now let $\alpha$ be irrational, so $|q\alpha-p|>0$ for every pair. Starting from one pair, choose $N$ larger than $1/|q\alpha-p|$; the new pair has a strictly smaller value of $|q\alpha-p|$. Repeating gives infinitely many pairs with values decreasing to $0$, each satisfying $|\alpha-\frac pq|<\frac1{q^2}$. They give infinitely many different fractions: the pairs representing one fraction $\frac{p_0}{q_0}$ in lowest terms are $(kp_0,kq_0)$ with $k\ge1$, and these have $|kq_0\alpha-kp_0|\ge|q_0\alpha-p_0|>0$, so only finitely many of our pairs can represent it.

blocks.title: Continued fractions find the best approximations
blocks.body:
Dirichlet's proof is not constructive, but [[continued-fractions|continued fractions]] produce the approximations explicitly. If $\alpha=[a_0;a_1,a_2,\dots]$ has convergents $\frac{p_n}{q_n}$, then
$$\frac{1}{q_n(q_n+q_{n+1})}<\Bigl|\alpha-\frac{p_n}{q_n}\Bigr|<\frac1{q_nq_{n+1}},\qquad q_{n+1}=a_{n+1}q_n+q_{n-1}.$$
So a large partial quotient $a_{n+1}$ means an unusually good approximation $\frac{p_n}{q_n}$. For $\pi=[3;7,15,1,292,\dots]$ the convergent $\frac{355}{113}$ is followed by $a_4=292$, which explains its accuracy.

Three further facts, all classical:
- Legendre: if $|\alpha-\frac pq|<\frac1{2q^2}$, then $\frac pq$ is a convergent of $\alpha$.
- Hurwitz: every irrational $\alpha$ has infinitely many $\frac pq$ with $|\alpha-\frac pq|<\frac1{\sqrt5\,q^2}$, and $\sqrt5$ cannot be replaced by any larger constant when $\alpha=\frac{1+\sqrt5}2=[1;1,1,\dots]$.
- $\alpha$ is badly approximable, meaning $|\alpha-\frac pq|>\frac c{q^2}$ for some $c>0$ and all $\frac pq$, exactly when its partial quotients are bounded. Quadratic irrationals have eventually periodic expansions and are therefore badly approximable.

So the exponent $2$ in Dirichlet's theorem cannot be improved for any quadratic irrational, and the constant matters only up to a bounded factor.

blocks.title: Liouville's theorem
blocks.body:
Let $\alpha$ be a real algebraic number of degree $d\ge2$. There is a constant $c(\alpha)>0$ such that
$$\Bigl|\alpha-\frac pq\Bigr|>\frac{c(\alpha)}{q^d}\qquad\text{for all integers }p\text{ and }q\ge1.$$
In particular $\mu(\alpha)\le d$.

Let $f\in\mathbb Z[x]$ be the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ with integer coefficients, of degree $d$. It is irreducible of degree at least $2$, so it has no rational roots, and $f(\frac pq)\ne0$. The number $q^df(\frac pq)$ is a nonzero integer, hence $|f(\frac pq)|\ge q^{-d}$.

Let $M=\max\{|f'(x)|:|x-\alpha|\le1\}$, which is positive. If $|\alpha-\frac pq|\le1$, the mean value theorem gives some $\xi$ between them with
$$q^{-d}\le\Bigl|f\Bigl(\frac pq\Bigr)\Bigr|=\Bigl|f(\alpha)-f\Bigl(\frac pq\Bigr)\Bigr|=|f'(\xi)|\,\Bigl|\alpha-\frac pq\Bigr|\le M\Bigl|\alpha-\frac pq\Bigr|.$$
If $|\alpha-\frac pq|>1$ then trivially $|\alpha-\frac pq|>q^{-d}$. So any $c(\alpha)<\min(1,1/M)$ works.

blocks.title: From Liouville to Roth
blocks.body:
Liouville's bound is easy because it uses only one polynomial. Improving the exponent $d$ needed a much deeper idea: construct an auxiliary polynomial in several variables that vanishes to high order at $(\alpha,\dots,\alpha)$, and show that two or more very good approximations would force it to vanish where it cannot. The history of the exponent for algebraic $\alpha$ of degree $d$:
- Liouville (1844): $d$.
- Thue (1909): $\frac d2+1+\varepsilon$.
- Siegel (1921): about $2\sqrt d$.
- Dyson (1947): about $\sqrt{2d}$.
- Roth (1955): $2+\varepsilon$, independent of $d$, which is best possible by Dirichlet. Roth received the Fields Medal in 1958.

blocks.title: Roth's theorem
blocks.body:
Let $\alpha$ be a real algebraic irrational number and $\varepsilon>0$. Then
$$\Bigl|\alpha-\frac pq\Bigr|<\frac{1}{q^{2+\varepsilon}}$$
has only finitely many solutions in rationals $\frac pq$ with $q\ge1$. Equivalently, $\mu(\alpha)=2$.

blocks.title: What Roth does not say
blocks.body:
Roth's theorem is ineffective: the proof shows there are finitely many exceptions but gives no way to bound them, so it cannot be used to list the solutions of an equation. Effective results with weaker exponents come from Baker's theory of linear forms in logarithms.

It also does not say whether $\varepsilon$ can be removed. For quadratic irrationals it can (they are badly approximable). For algebraic numbers of degree at least $3$, such as $\sqrt[3]2$, it is unknown whether the partial quotients are bounded; no example is known either way.

The exponent $2$ is not special to algebraic numbers. Khintchine's theorem says that if $\psi$ is positive and non-increasing, then for almost every real $\alpha$ the inequality $|q\alpha-p|<\psi(q)$ has infinitely many solutions if $\sum_q\psi(q)$ diverges, and only finitely many if it converges. With $\psi(q)=q^{-1-\varepsilon}$ the series converges, so almost every $\alpha$ has $\mu(\alpha)=2$. The Duffin–Schaeffer conjecture, a version without monotonicity for reduced fractions, was proved by Koukoulopoulos and Maynard (2020). The exceptional set $\{\alpha:\mu(\alpha)\ge\tau\}$ has Lebesgue measure zero for $\tau>2$ and Hausdorff dimension $2/\tau$ (Jarník, Besicovitch).

blocks.title: Irrationality proofs are approximation statements
blocks.body: Turn the question around. Rationals are very badly approximated by other rationals: if $\alpha=\frac ab$ and $\frac pq\ne\alpha$, then $|\alpha-\frac pq|=\frac{|aq-bp|}{bq}\ge\frac1{bq}$. This gives a criterion for irrationality.

blocks.title: Irrationality criterion
blocks.body:
Let $\alpha$ be real. If there are integers $p_n,q_n$ with $q_n\alpha-p_n\ne0$ for all $n$ and $q_n\alpha-p_n\to0$, then $\alpha$ is irrational.

Quantitative form: if moreover $\frac1n\log|q_n|\to\log Q$ and $\frac1n\log|q_n\alpha-p_n|\to-\log E$ with $Q>1$ and $E>1$, then $\mu(\alpha)\le1+\frac{\log Q}{\log E}$.

blocks.title: Proof of the qualitative criterion
blocks.body: Suppose $\alpha=\frac ab$ with $b\ge1$. Then $b(q_n\alpha-p_n)=aq_n-bp_n$ is a nonzero integer, so $|q_n\alpha-p_n|\ge\frac1b$ for all $n$, contradicting $q_n\alpha-p_n\to0$. (The quantitative form is proved by comparing a hypothetical very good approximation $\frac pq$ with the forms $q_n\alpha-p_n$ for a suitably chosen $n$; we omit it.)

blocks.title: Two irrationality proofs
blocks.body:
The number $e$. Let $q_n=n!$ and $p_n=n!\sum_{k\le n}\frac1{k!}$, an integer. Then
$$0<q_ne-p_n=\sum_{k>n}\frac{n!}{k!}=\frac1{n+1}+\frac1{(n+1)(n+2)}+\cdots<\sum_{j\ge1}\frac1{(n+1)^j}=\frac1n,$$
so $e$ is irrational by the criterion. (Here $q_n$ grows faster than exponentially, so the quantitative form does not apply; in fact $\mu(e)=2$, which follows from its explicit continued fraction $[2;1,2,1,1,4,1,1,6,\dots]$.)

Apéry's theorem (1978): $\zeta(3)$ is irrational. Apéry found integers $a_n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk^2\binom{n+k}k^2$ and rationals $b_n$ with $2\,d_n^3b_n\in\mathbb Z$, where $d_n=\mathrm{lcm}(1,\dots,n)$, such that
$$0<|a_n\zeta(3)-b_n|\ \text{decays like}\ (1+\sqrt2)^{-4n},\qquad a_n\ \text{grows like}\ (1+\sqrt2)^{4n},$$
up to polynomial factors; both satisfy $n^3u_n=(34n^3-51n^2+27n-5)u_{n-1}-(n-1)^3u_{n-2}$. By the prime number theorem $d_n=e^{n(1+o(1))}$. Put $q_n=2d_n^3a_n$ and $p_n=2d_n^3b_n$. Then $|q_n|$ grows like $Q^n$ with $Q=e^3(1+\sqrt2)^4$ and $|q_n\zeta(3)-p_n|$ decays like $E^{-n}$ with $E=(1+\sqrt2)^4/e^3$. The key numerical fact is $E>1$: $4\log(1+\sqrt2)\approx3.5255>3$. So $\zeta(3)$ is irrational, and the quantitative criterion gives $\mu(\zeta(3))\le1+\frac{3+4\log(1+\sqrt2)}{4\log(1+\sqrt2)-3}\approx13.42$. No analogous construction is known for $\zeta(5)$. Later work showed that infinitely many of the values $\zeta(3),\zeta(5),\zeta(7),\dots$ are irrational (Ball and Rivoal) and that at least one of $\zeta(5),\zeta(7),\zeta(9),\zeta(11)$ is irrational (Zudilin), but no specific odd value beyond $\zeta(3)$ is known to be irrational.

blocks.title: Example 1: approximating √2
blocks.body: The convergents of $\sqrt2=[1;2,2,2,\dots]$ are $1,\frac32,\frac75,\frac{17}{12},\frac{41}{29},\frac{99}{70},\dots$ Show that each satisfies $p^2-2q^2=\pm1$, and deduce that $q^2|\sqrt2-\frac pq|\to\frac1{2\sqrt2}\approx0.354$.
blocks.solution:
The convergents satisfy $p_{n+1}=2p_n+p_{n-1}$, $q_{n+1}=2q_n+q_{n-1}$; equivalently $p_{n+1}+q_{n+1}\sqrt2=(p_n+q_n\sqrt2)(1+\sqrt2)$. Since $(1+\sqrt2)(1-\sqrt2)=-1$, the norm $p^2-2q^2$ changes sign at each step and keeps absolute value $1$: $1-2=-1$, $9-8=1$, $49-50=-1$, $289-288=1$, $1681-1682=-1$, $9801-9800=1$. These are the solutions of [[pell|Pell's equation]] $p^2-2q^2=\pm1$.

Then $|p-q\sqrt2|=\frac{|p^2-2q^2|}{p+q\sqrt2}=\frac1{p+q\sqrt2}$, so
$$q^2\Bigl|\sqrt2-\frac pq\Bigr|=\frac{q}{p+q\sqrt2}=\frac{1}{p/q+\sqrt2}\to\frac1{2\sqrt2}.$$
For $\frac{99}{70}$ the value is $0.35354\ldots$. So $\sqrt2$ is approximated to order exactly $q^{-2}$, never better: it is badly approximable, as every quadratic irrational is.

blocks.title: Example 2: |sin n| is often small
blocks.body: Prove that there are infinitely many positive integers $n$ with $|\sin n|<\frac5n$.
blocks.solution:
By Dirichlet's theorem applied to $\pi$ there are infinitely many fractions $\frac nm$ with $m\ge1$ and $|\pi-\frac nm|<\frac1{m^2}$, i.e. $|m\pi-n|<\frac1m$. Since $\sin$ has period $\pi$ up to sign and $|\sin x|\le|x|$,
$$|\sin n|=|\sin(n-m\pi)|\le|n-m\pi|<\frac1m.$$
Also $n<m\pi+\frac1m\le m(\pi+1)<5m$, so $\frac1m<\frac5n$. As the fractions are distinct and $|\frac nm-\pi|\to0$, the denominators $m$ are unbounded and hence so are the $n\approx m\pi$; infinitely many $n$ occur.

For instance $n=355$: $355\,|\sin355|\approx0.0107$, far below $5$.

blocks.title: Example 3: Liouville's number is transcendental
blocks.body: Let $\lambda=\sum_{k\ge1}10^{-k!}=0.110001000\ldots$. Show that $\lambda$ is not algebraic.
blocks.solution:
Let $q_n=10^{n!}$ and $p_n=q_n\sum_{k\le n}10^{-k!}$, an integer. Since $(n+1)!+j\le(n+1+j)!$ for $j\ge0$, the tail satisfies
$$0<\lambda-\frac{p_n}{q_n}=\sum_{k>n}10^{-k!}\le10^{-(n+1)!}\sum_{j\ge0}10^{-j}=\frac{10}{9}\,10^{-(n+1)!}<\frac{2}{q_n^{\,n+1}}.$$
If $\lambda$ were algebraic of degree $d\ge2$, Liouville's theorem would give $\frac{c}{q_n^d}<\frac{2}{q_n^{n+1}}$, i.e. $q_n^{\,n+1-d}<\frac2c$, false for large $n$. If $\lambda$ were rational, $\lambda=\frac ab$, then $\lambda-\frac{p_n}{q_n}\ne0$ would be at least $\frac1{bq_n}$, again contradicting the bound for large $n$. So $\lambda$ is transcendental, with $\mu(\lambda)=\infty$.

blocks.title: Example 4: a Thue equation
blocks.body: Let $m\ne0$ be an integer. Show that $x^3-2y^3=m$ has only finitely many integer solutions.
blocks.solution:
Let $\theta=\sqrt[3]2$ and $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$. Over $\mathbb C$,
$$x^3-2y^3=(x-\theta y)(x-\omega\theta y)(x-\omega^2\theta y).$$
For $y\ne0$ and $j=1,2$, the imaginary part of $x-\omega^j\theta y$ is $\mp\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\theta y$, so $|x-\omega^j\theta y|\ge\frac{\sqrt3}2\theta|y|$. Hence
$$|x-\theta y|\le\frac{|m|}{\frac34\theta^2y^2},\qquad\Bigl|\theta-\frac xy\Bigr|\le\frac{4|m|}{3\theta^2|y|^3}.$$
For $|y|$ large the right side is smaller than $|y|^{-5/2}$. By Roth's theorem with $\varepsilon=\frac12$ (Thue's exponent $\frac32+1+\varepsilon<3$ already suffices) only finitely many fractions $\frac xy$ satisfy this. Each fraction $\frac{x_0}{y_0}$ in lowest terms gives solutions $(kx_0,ky_0)$ only when $k^3\mid m$, so finitely many $k$. Solutions with $y=0$ need $x^3=m$, at most one. Hence finitely many solutions in total.

For $m=1$ a search over $|x|,|y|\le200$ finds only $(1,0)$ and $(-1,-1)$. The argument cannot prove the list is complete, because Roth's theorem is ineffective; completing it needs effective methods.

blocks.body:
- Roth's theorem needs $\alpha$ irrational. For rational $\alpha=\frac ab$ the pairs $(ka,kb)$ give $|\alpha-\frac pq|=0$ infinitely often, which is why the definition of $\mu$ requires $0<|\alpha-\frac pq|$.
- Exponent $2$ does not make a number algebraic: almost every real number has $\mu=2$. Only $\mu>2$ rules out algebraicity.
- Most transcendental numbers, including $e$ and $\pi$, are not Liouville numbers; Liouville's method proves transcendence only for very special numbers.
- "Infinitely often" is not "for all $q$": for most $q$ the best approximation is only of order $\frac1q$.
- Roth's theorem is ineffective; it cannot be used to find all solutions of an equation.

[[continued-fractions]] are the computational heart of the subject, and [[pell|Pell's equation]] is the statement that quadratic irrationals have approximations of exact order $q^{-2}$. Approximation theorems give finiteness results for [[diophantine|Diophantine equations]]: Thue equations directly, and integral points on curves, including [[elliptic-curves]], through Siegel's theorem. Dirichlet's theorem is the first step in splitting the circle into major and minor arcs in the [[circle-method]] and in bounding [[exponential-sums]] such as Weyl sums. The distribution of $\{n\alpha\}$ modulo $1$, measured by [[discrepancy]], is controlled by the partial quotients of $\alpha$. Irrationality of values of the [[zeta|zeta function]] is the most famous application of the criterion.

1. Show that $\mu(\alpha)=1$ for every rational $\alpha$.
2. Use Dirichlet's theorem to show that for irrational $\alpha$ the set $\{\{n\alpha\}:n\ge1\}$ is dense in $[0,1)$.
3. Show that if the partial quotients of $\alpha$ are bounded by $K$, then $|\alpha-\frac pq|>\frac{1}{(K+2)q^2}$ for all convergents $\frac pq$.
4. Use Roth's theorem to show that $\sum_{k\ge0}2^{-3^k}$ is transcendental.

blocks.body:
The [[fta|fundamental theorem of arithmetic]] lets us sort integers by the shape of their factorisation. Three shapes come up again and again. Numbers all of whose prime factors are small (smooth numbers) are what factoring algorithms hunt for. Numbers in which every prime appears at least squared (powerful numbers) are where the abc conjecture has its bite. Numbers in which no prime appears twice (squarefree numbers) are the typical case and the support of the Möbius function.

For each class we ask: how many are there up to $x$? The answers are three quite different asymptotic laws, $\rho(u)x$, $c\sqrt x$ and $\frac6{\pi^2}x$, and each has a short proof that shows a useful technique.

blocks.title: Smooth, powerful and squarefree numbers
blocks.body:
Let $P(n)$ be the largest prime factor of $n$, with $P(1)=1$.
- $n$ is $y$-smooth if $P(n)\le y$. Write $\Psi(x,y)=\#\{n\le x:P(n)\le y\}$.
- $n$ is powerful (also called squarefull) if $p\mid n\Rightarrow p^2\mid n$ for every prime $p$.
- $n$ is squarefree if $p^2\nmid n$ for every prime $p$; equivalently $\mu(n)\ne0$.

The number $1$ belongs to all three classes. Smoothness depends on a parameter $y$; the other two are absolute properties of the exponents in the factorisation.

blocks.title: Squarefree numbers: inclusion–exclusion with squares
blocks.body:
Each $n\ge1$ can be written uniquely as $n=a^2b$ with $b$ squarefree: put each prime with an even exponent entirely into $a^2$, and for a prime with an odd exponent $e$ put $p^{e-1}$ into $a^2$ and $p$ into $b$. Then $d^2\mid n$ exactly when $d\mid a$, so by the basic property of the Möbius function ([[mobius]])
$$\sum_{d^2\mid n}\mu(d)=\sum_{d\mid a}\mu(d)=\begin{cases}1,&a=1,\\0,&a>1,\end{cases}$$
which is $1$ exactly when $n$ is squarefree. In other words $\mu(n)^2=\sum_{d^2\mid n}\mu(d)$. This is the sieve of Eratosthenes run with the squares $4,9,25,\dots$ instead of the primes.

blocks.title: Counting squarefree numbers
blocks.body:
Let $Q(x)$ be the number of squarefree $n\le x$. Then
$$Q(x)=\frac{6}{\pi^2}\,x+O(\sqrt x).$$

Sum the identity $\mu(n)^2=\sum_{d^2\mid n}\mu(d)$ over $n\le x$ and swap the order of summation. The multiples of $d^2$ up to $x$ number $\lfloor x/d^2\rfloor$, and only $d\le\sqrt x$ contribute:
$$Q(x)=\sum_{d\le\sqrt x}\mu(d)\Bigl\lfloor\frac{x}{d^2}\Bigr\rfloor=x\sum_{d\le\sqrt x}\frac{\mu(d)}{d^2}+O(\sqrt x),$$
since each floor differs from $x/d^2$ by less than $1$. The full series is $\sum_{d\ge1}\mu(d)d^{-2}=1/\zeta(2)=6/\pi^2$ ([[zeta]]), and the tail is $\bigl|\sum_{d>\sqrt x}\mu(d)d^{-2}\bigr|\le\sum_{d>\sqrt x}d^{-2}\le\frac{1}{\sqrt x-1}$ for $x>1$. Multiplying by $x$ gives another $O(\sqrt x)$.

blocks.title: Powerful numbers: a parametrisation
blocks.body: Powerful numbers are much rarer, about $\sqrt x$ of them up to $x$, because they are close to squares. Every square is powerful, and so is every number $a^2b^3$. Conversely, every powerful $n$ is of this form, and uniquely so if we insist that $b$ is squarefree: for each prime $p$ dividing $n$ with exponent $e\ge2$, if $e$ is even put $p^e$ into $a^2$; if $e$ is odd (so $e\ge3$) put $p^3$ into $b^3$ and $p^{e-3}$ into $a^2$. The squarefree $b$ must be the product of the primes appearing to an odd power, since in $a^2b^3$ the exponent of $p$ is $2v_p(a)+3[p\mid b]$, which is odd exactly when $p\mid b$. So $b$ and then $a$ are determined.

blocks.title: Counting powerful numbers
blocks.body:
Let $P_2(x)$ be the number of powerful $n\le x$. Then
$$P_2(x)=\frac{\zeta(3/2)}{\zeta(3)}\sqrt x+O(x^{1/3}),\qquad\frac{\zeta(3/2)}{\zeta(3)}\approx2.1733.$$

By the parametrisation, $P_2(x)$ counts pairs $(a,b)$ with $b$ squarefree and $a^2b^3\le x$. For fixed $b$ there are $\lfloor\sqrt{x/b^3}\rfloor$ choices of $a$, and $b\le x^{1/3}$. So
$$P_2(x)=\sum_{\substack{b\le x^{1/3}\\ b\text{ squarefree}}}\Bigl\lfloor\frac{\sqrt x}{b^{3/2}}\Bigr\rfloor=\sqrt x\sum_{\substack{b\le x^{1/3}\\ b\text{ squarefree}}}b^{-3/2}+O(x^{1/3}).$$
The series over all squarefree $b$ has Euler product $\prod_p(1+p^{-3/2})=\prod_p\frac{1-p^{-3}}{1-p^{-3/2}}=\frac{\zeta(3/2)}{\zeta(3)}$, and its tail beyond $x^{1/3}$ is at most $\sum_{b>x^{1/3}}b^{-3/2}\ll x^{-1/6}$, which contributes $O(\sqrt x\cdot x^{-1/6})=O(x^{1/3})$.

blocks.title: Smooth numbers and Dickman's function
blocks.body:
Now fix $u\ge1$ and count $n\le x$ with all prime factors at most $x^{1/u}$. The answer is a positive proportion of $x$, but the proportion falls very fast with $u$.

For $1\le u\le2$ it is easy. A number $n\le x$ can have at most one prime factor $p>x^{1/u}\ge\sqrt x$, since two would multiply to more than $x$. So the numbers that are not $x^{1/u}$-smooth are counted exactly once each by
$$x-\Psi(x,x^{1/u})=\sum_{x^{1/u}<p\le x}\Bigl\lfloor\frac xp\Bigr\rfloor=x\sum_{x^{1/u}<p\le x}\frac1p+O(\pi(x)).$$
By Mertens' theorem $\sum_{p\le t}\frac1p=\log\log t+M+O(1/\log t)$ ([[mertens]]), the sum of $1/p$ equals $\log\log x-\log\log x^{1/u}+o(1)=\log u+o(1)$. Since $\pi(x)=o(x)$, we get
$$\Psi(x,x^{1/u})=(1-\log u+o(1))\,x\qquad(1\le u\le2).$$
In particular about $1-\log2\approx30.7\%$ of integers have no prime factor above their square root.

For larger $u$ the same idea, applied recursively (remove the largest prime factor $p$ and count the cofactor, which is $p$-smooth and at most $x/p$), leads to the identity $\Psi(x,y)=\Psi(x,z)-\sum_{y<p\le z}\Psi(x/p,p)$ for $y<z$, and in the limit to a delay differential equation.

blocks.title: Dickman's theorem
blocks.body:
Let $\rho$ be the continuous function on $[0,\infty)$ with $\rho(u)=1$ for $0\le u\le1$ and
$$u\rho'(u)=-\rho(u-1)\qquad(u>1).$$
Then for every fixed $u\ge1$,
$$\Psi(x,x^{1/u})\sim\rho(u)\,x\qquad(x\to\infty).$$
Moreover $\rho(u)=u^{-u(1+o(1))}$ as $u\to\infty$.

blocks.title: The size of ρ and why factoring cares
blocks.body:
From the differential equation, $\rho(u)=1-\log u$ on $[1,2]$, and numerically
$$\rho(2)\approx0.3069,\quad\rho(3)\approx0.0486,\quad\rho(4)\approx0.00491,\quad\rho(5)\approx3.55\times10^{-4},\quad\rho(10)\approx2.77\times10^{-11}.$$
The rough rule $\rho(u)\approx u^{-u}$ explains the decay: a number is $x^{1/u}$-smooth roughly when it splits into $u$ pieces of size $x^{1/u}$, and each piece is a "coincidence" of probability about $1/u$.

An upper bound of the right flavour is easy (Rankin's trick): for any $\sigma>0$,
$$\Psi(x,y)\le\sum_{P(n)\le y}\Bigl(\frac xn\Bigr)^{\sigma}=x^{\sigma}\prod_{p\le y}\bigl(1-p^{-\sigma}\bigr)^{-1},$$
because each term with $n\le x$ is at least $1$ and the others are positive. Optimising $\sigma$ already gives bounds of the shape $x\,u^{-u(1+o(1))}$ in wide ranges.

Factoring. To factor $N$, the quadratic sieve looks for many $x$ such that $x^2-N$ (or $x^2\bmod N$) is $y$-smooth. Once there are more such numbers than primes up to $y$, linear algebra modulo $2$ finds a product that is a perfect square, giving $a^2\equiv b^2\pmod N$, and $\gcd(a-b,N)$ is often a proper factor. A larger $y$ makes smooth values more common but requires more of them; balancing the two with Dickman's function gives running time $\exp\bigl((1+o(1))\sqrt{\log N\log\log N}\bigr)$. The number field sieve uses smaller numbers to test for smoothness and reaches $\exp\bigl(O((\log N)^{1/3}(\log\log N)^{2/3})\bigr)$. The same smoothness counts govern index-calculus attacks on the [[discrete-log|discrete logarithm problem]] and hence the key sizes for [[rsa|RSA]].

blocks.title: Example 1: checking the laws at x = 10^6
blocks.body: Compare $Q(10^6)$ and $P_2(10^6)$ with the main terms of the theorems.
blocks.solution:
Direct counting gives $Q(10^6)=607926$, against $\frac6{\pi^2}10^6\approx607927.1$, an error of about $1$, far inside the $O(10^3)$ allowed.

For powerful numbers, $P_2(10^6)=2027$, against $\frac{\zeta(3/2)}{\zeta(3)}\cdot1000\approx2173.3$. The difference of about $-146$ is comparable to $x^{1/3}=100$, as the error term allows. In fact a finer analysis (Bateman and Grosswald) gives the second term $\frac{\zeta(2/3)}{\zeta(2)}x^{1/3}$, and $\zeta(2/3)\approx-2.447$ is negative; with it the prediction becomes $2173.3-148.8\approx2024.5$, within $3$ of the true count.

blocks.title: Example 2: smooth numbers converge slowly
blocks.body: Compute $\Psi(10^6,10^3)$ and $\Psi(10^6,10^2)$ and compare with $\rho(2)x$ and $\rho(3)x$.
blocks.solution:
A sieve for the largest prime factor gives $\Psi(10^6,1000)=344299$ and $\Psi(10^6,100)=72271$, that is $34.4\%$ and $7.2\%$, against $\rho(2)\approx30.7\%$ and $\rho(3)\approx4.9\%$.

The asymptotic is correct but the convergence is slow: the relative error behaves like a constant over $\log y$, and $\log 1000\approx6.9$ is small. For $u=3$ the true proportion is about $1.5$ times $\rho(3)$. In applications (for instance when tuning a factoring algorithm) one uses more precise approximations or computes $\Psi$ directly.

blocks.title: Example 3: consecutive powerful numbers
blocks.body: Show that there are infinitely many pairs of consecutive integers that are both powerful.
blocks.solution:
Consider [[pell|Pell's equation]] $x^2-8y^2=1$. It has the solution $(3,1)$, and from any solution $(x,y)$ we get the larger solution $(3x+8y,\,x+3y)$, since $(3x+8y)^2-8(x+3y)^2=x^2-8y^2$. So there are infinitely many solutions with $y\ge1$.

For each solution, $8y^2=2^3y^2$ is powerful: $2$ appears to an exponent at least $3$, and every other prime divides $y^2$ to an even, hence at least second, power. And $x^2=8y^2+1$ is a square, hence powerful. So $8y^2$ and $8y^2+1$ are consecutive powerful numbers. The first few pairs are $(8,9)$, $(288,289)$, $(9800,9801)$.

Erdős conjectured that there are no three consecutive powerful numbers; this is open.

blocks.title: Example 4: smoothness as a probability
blocks.body: Roughly what fraction of integers near $10^{100}$ have no prime factor above $10^{20}$? Compare $\rho(u)$ with the rule of thumb $u^{-u}$.
blocks.solution:
Here $u=\frac{\log10^{100}}{\log10^{20}}=5$, so Dickman's theorem suggests a proportion of about $\rho(5)\approx3.5\times10^{-4}$, about one in $2800$. The crude rule gives $5^{-5}=3.2\times10^{-4}$, the same order of magnitude. (Example 2 shows that the true proportion at finite height is somewhat larger than $\rho(u)$, but with $\log y\approx46$ the correction is much smaller than at $y=100$.)

So among random 100-digit numbers, smooth ones are rare but far from impossible to find; this is what makes the sieve methods practical.

blocks.body:
- Dickman's asymptotic is for fixed $u$ (that is, $y$ a fixed power of $x$). When $y$ is a power of $\log x$ the behaviour is different: $\Psi(x,(\log x)^A)=x^{1-1/A+o(1)}$ for fixed $A>1$.
- Powerful is not the same as being a perfect power: $72=2^3\cdot3^2$ is powerful but not a perfect power, and both classes have about $\sqrt x$ members up to $x$ but with different constants.
- The density of squarefree numbers is $\frac6{\pi^2}\approx0.608$, not $\prod_p(1-\frac1p)$, which is $0$. Squarefreeness restricts each prime a little ($1-p^{-2}$), not much.
- Do not plug finite $x$ into $\rho(u)x$ and expect accuracy (Example 2).
- $1$ is smooth, powerful and squarefree; formulas are stated with that convention.

The squarefree count is the simplest example of a sieve with Möbius weights ([[mobius]], [[sieve-basics]]); the constant is $1/\zeta(2)$ and the whole subject is driven by Euler products ([[zeta]]). Smooth number estimates rest on [[mertens|Mertens' theorems]] and are central to computational number theory: factoring, [[primality|primality testing]] analyses, [[rsa]] and the [[discrete-log|discrete logarithm]]. They are also an ingredient in constructing large gaps between primes ([[prime-patterns]]), where one needs few smooth numbers in an interval, and in [[probabilistic-nt|probabilistic number theory]], where the largest prime factor of a random integer has a limiting distribution described by $\rho$. Powerful numbers have small radical ($\mathrm{rad}(n)\le\sqrt n$), which is exactly what the abc conjecture controls; [[pell|Pell equations]] produce the consecutive pairs.

1. Show that the density of odd squarefree numbers is $\frac4{\pi^2}$.
2. Show that $\mathrm{rad}(n)\le\sqrt n$ for powerful $n$, where $\mathrm{rad}(n)$ is the product of the distinct primes dividing $n$, with equality exactly when $n$ is the square of a squarefree number.
3. Show that $\Psi(x,3)\sim\frac{(\log x)^2}{2\log2\log3}$.
4. Use the differential equation to write $\rho(u)$ on $[2,3]$ as an explicit integral, and evaluate $\rho(3)$ numerically.
