blocks.body:
The [[pnt|prime number theorem]] describes primes on average: about $x/\log x$ of them up to $x$, so near $x$ consecutive primes are about $\log x$ apart. Almost every finer question is open. Does $n^2+1$ take infinitely many prime values? How large can the gap after a prime $p$ be, compared with $\log p$? Does every interval $[x,x+\sqrt x]$ contain a prime?

This lesson collects what is proved and what is believed about three related themes: primes in special sequences, large and small gaps between consecutive primes, and primes in short intervals. The proved results come from sieves ([[sieve-basics]]), from zeros of $\zeta$, and from combinatorial constructions with residue classes; the beliefs come mostly from random models.

blocks.title: Prime gaps
blocks.body:
Let $p_1=2<p_2=3<\cdots$ be the primes and $g_n=p_{n+1}-p_n$ the $n$-th prime gap. The maximal gap up to $x$ is
$$G(x)=\max_{p_{n+1}\le x}(p_{n+1}-p_n).$$
A gap $g_n$ is called maximal (or a record) if it is larger than all earlier gaps. The natural unit for gaps near $x$ is $\log x$, the average spacing.

blocks.title: Gaps are log p on average
blocks.body: $$\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{g_n}{\log p_n}\le1\le\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{g_n}{\log p_n}.$$

Fix $\eta\in(0,1)$ and let $x$ be large. Consider the primes in $(x^{1-\eta},x]$; let $p_a$ be the first and $p_b$ the last. By the prime number theorem the number of gaps $g_a,\dots,g_{b-1}$ between them is $b-a=\pi(x)-\pi(x^{1-\eta})-1=(1+o(1))\frac{x}{\log x}$, and they telescope:
$$\sum_{n=a}^{b-1}g_n=p_b-p_a.$$
For these $n$, $(1-\eta)\log x<\log p_n\le\log x$.

Suppose the first inequality fails: then there are $c>1$ and $n_0$ with $g_n\ge c\log p_n$ for $n\ge n_0$. For large $x$ every term above is at least $c(1-\eta)\log x$, so $x\ge p_b-p_a\ge c(1-\eta)\log x\cdot(1+o(1))\frac{x}{\log x}$, giving $c(1-\eta)\le1$. As $\eta$ is arbitrary, $c\le1$, a contradiction.

Suppose the second fails: then $g_n\le c\log p_n$ for $n\ge n_0$ with some $c<1$. Then every gap after $p_{n_0}$ is at most $c\log x$ when $p_{n+1}\le x$, so in particular $p_a\le x^{1-\eta}+c\log x$ and $p_b\ge x-c\log x$. Hence $p_b-p_a\ge x-2x^{1-\eta}$, while the sum is at most $c\log x\cdot(1+o(1))\frac x{\log x}=(c+o(1))x$. So $1\le c$, a contradiction.

blocks.title: Long gaps: covering an interval with residue classes
blocks.body:
The first idea is the classic one: $(k+1)!+2,(k+1)!+3,\dots,(k+1)!+(k+1)$ are $k$ consecutive composites, since $(k+1)!+j$ is divisible by $j$. This gives gaps of length $k$ near $(k+1)!$, which is about $e^{k\log k}$, so only $G(x)\gtrsim\log x/\log\log x$, worse than the average.

The better idea is to separate the two jobs. Choose a residue class $a_p\bmod p$ for each prime $p\le y$, so that every integer in $[1,z]$ lies in at least one chosen class. By the [[crt|Chinese remainder theorem]] there is $N$ with $y<N\le y+\prod_{p\le y}p=e^{(1+o(1))y}$ and $N\equiv-a_p\pmod p$ for all $p\le y$. Then each of $N+1,\dots,N+z$ is divisible by some $p\le y$, and all exceed $y$, so they are composite: a gap of length at least $z$ below about $e^{y}$. Taking $a_p=0$ for all $p$ covers $[2,y]$, and the same argument then gives $y-1$ consecutive composites below about $e^{y}$: only a gap of the average size $\log x$. Everything depends on covering a much longer interval $[1,z]$ with $z\gg y$.

The Erdős–Rankin method does this in three stages. First, give the class $0\bmod p$ to every prime $p$ in a middle range $(w,\,y/2]$. A number in $[1,z]$ survives this only if all its prime factors are $\le w$ or $>y/2$: either it is $w$-smooth, and smooth numbers are rare ([[smooth-powerful]]), or it has the form $mq$ with $q>y/2$ prime and $m\le 2z/y$ small. Second, choose the classes of the small primes $p\le w$ so as to remove as many of the numbers $mq$ as possible; since the $q$ behave like random primes, a good choice for $p$ removes about a fraction $1/p$ of them, and together the small primes cut them down by a factor of about $\prod_{p\le w}(1-\frac1p)\asymp\frac1{\log w}$. Third, the few survivors left are covered one at a time by the unused primes in $(y/2,y]$, each of which can be given a class containing one survivor. Balancing the three stages determines how large $z$ can be; it is the same kind of combinatorics as in [[covering-systems]].

blocks.title: Large gaps
blocks.body:
1. Westzynthius (1931): $\displaystyle\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{g_n}{\log p_n}=\infty$.
2. Rankin (1938): for some $c>0$ and all large $x$, $\displaystyle G(x)\ge c\,\frac{\log x\,\log\log x\,\log\log\log\log x}{(\log\log\log x)^2}$.
3. Ford, Green, Konyagin, Maynard and Tao (2018): for some $c>0$ and all large $x$, $\displaystyle G(x)\ge c\,\frac{\log x\,\log\log x\,\log\log\log\log x}{\log\log\log x}$.

The last result removes one factor of $\log\log\log x$ from Rankin's bound; earlier, Ford–Green–Konyagin–Tao and Maynard had independently shown that Rankin's constant $c$ can be taken arbitrarily large. The new ingredient is a way of choosing the residue classes for the medium-sized primes so that they hit many more of the survivors, built with tools from the work on [[bounded-gaps|bounded gaps]].

blocks.title: Upper bounds: primes in short intervals
blocks.body:
In the other direction one wants every interval $(x,x+h]$ to contain a prime, with $h$ as small as possible.
- Bertrand's postulate (Chebyshev, 1852): $h=x$ suffices.
- Hoheisel (1930) first obtained $h=x^{\theta}$ with $\theta<1$. The method is the one in [[zero-density]]: density estimates for zeros of $\zeta$ and a zero-free region give $\psi(x+x^\theta)-\psi(x)\sim x^\theta$ for $\theta>1-1/A$. Huxley's density theorem gives $\theta>\tfrac7{12}$ for this asymptotic.
- Baker, Harman and Pintz (2001), adding sieve methods that give a lower bound rather than an asymptotic: $g_n\ll p_n^{0.525}$.
- Assuming the [[rh|Riemann hypothesis]], Cramér (1920) proved $g_n\ll\sqrt{p_n}\log p_n$.

Even RH does not give a prime between consecutive squares $n^2$ and $(n+1)^2$ (Legendre's conjecture), since that needs $g_n\ll\sqrt{p_n}$ without the logarithm.

What is believed is much stronger. Cramér modelled the primes as a random set containing each $n\ge3$ independently with probability $1/\log n$. In that model the largest gap up to $x$ is about $(\log x)^2$, which led to Cramér's conjecture $g_n=O((\log p_n)^2)$. The model ignores divisibility by small primes; Granville argued that correcting this suggests $\limsup g_n/(\log p_n)^2\ge2e^{-\gamma}\approx1.12$ rather than $1$. Maier (1985) showed that the Cramér model really does fail in short intervals: for every fixed $\lambda>1$ the number of primes in $(x,x+(\log x)^\lambda]$ is not asymptotic to $(\log x)^{\lambda-1}$, the oscillation being of fixed relative size in both directions.

blocks.title: Small gaps and patterns
blocks.body:
Small gaps are the subject of [[bounded-gaps]]: Zhang (2013) proved $\liminf g_n<7\times10^7$, Maynard and Tao reduced the bound and showed that any number of primes occur infinitely often within bounded distance, and the current bound is $246$. The [[twin-primes|twin prime conjecture]] $\liminf g_n=2$ remains open.

For primes in arithmetic progressions, Dirichlet's theorem gives infinitely many primes $\equiv a\pmod q$ when $\gcd(a,q)=1$ ([[l-functions]]). Green and Tao (2004) proved that the primes contain arithmetic progressions of every finite length, by a relative version of Szemerédi's theorem ([[arithmetic-progressions]]) applied to a pseudorandom majorant of the primes.

For polynomial sequences almost nothing is known in one variable. Landau's question whether $n^2+1$ is prime infinitely often is open; Iwaniec (1978) showed that $n^2+1$ has at most two prime factors for infinitely many $n$. With two variables, sparse prime-rich sequences have been reached: Friedlander and Iwaniec (1998) proved that infinitely many primes have the form $a^2+b^4$, and Heath-Brown (2001) did the same for $x^3+2y^3$.

The obstruction to proving that a sequence contains primes, rather than numbers with few prime factors, is the parity problem of sieve theory: sieve weights cannot distinguish numbers with an odd number of prime factors from those with an even number. This is why Chen's theorem (every large even number is $p+P_2$, with $P_2$ having at most two prime factors) is the natural limit of pure sieve methods for [[goldbach|Goldbach]]-type problems, and why the results above need extra arithmetic input.

blocks.title: Example 1: k consecutive composites
blocks.body: Show that for every $k$ there are $k$ consecutive composite numbers, and compare the size of the factorial construction with the actual first occurrence of a gap of length at least $72$.
blocks.solution:
For $2\le j\le k+1$, $j$ divides both $(k+1)!$ and $j$, hence divides $(k+1)!+j$, which is larger than $j$. So $(k+1)!+2,\dots,(k+1)!+k+1$ are $k$ consecutive composites.

For a run of $71$ composites (a gap of $72$) the construction uses numbers near $72!\approx6.1\times10^{103}$. The first gap of length at least $72$ actually occurs after the prime $31397$: the next prime is $31469$. The factorial method is wildly wasteful, because it uses a different prime power for every position instead of letting one prime cover many positions.

blocks.title: Example 2: prime progressions need special differences
blocks.body: Let $a,a+d,\dots,a+(k-1)d$ be primes with $d\ge1$ and $a>k$. Prove that $d$ is divisible by every prime $p\le k$. Check the example $7,37,67,97,127,157$.
blocks.solution:
Let $p\le k$ be prime and suppose $p\nmid d$. Then $d$ is invertible modulo $p$, so the $p$ numbers $a,a+d,\dots,a+(p-1)d$ (all in the progression, since $p\le k$) lie in distinct residue classes modulo $p$, hence in all of them. One is divisible by $p$; being at least $a>k\ge p$, it is not equal to $p$, so it is composite. Contradiction; hence $p\mid d$.

In the example $k=6$, $a=7>6$, and $d=30$ is divisible by $2,3,5$, as it must be; all six terms are prime. The hypothesis $a>k$ matters: $5,11,17,23,29$ has $k=5$ and $d=6$, not divisible by $5$, which is possible only because the first term is $5$ itself.

blocks.title: Example 3: record gaps against (log p)²
blocks.body: Some maximal gaps: $72$ after $31397$, $114$ after $492113$, and $1132$ after $1693182318746371$. Compute $g/\log p$ and $g/(\log p)^2$ for each.
blocks.solution:
- $p=31397$: $\log p\approx10.35$, so $g/\log p\approx6.95$ and $g/(\log p)^2\approx0.672$.
- $p=492113$: $\log p\approx13.11$, so $g/\log p\approx8.70$ and $g/(\log p)^2\approx0.664$.
- $p=1693182318746371$: $\log p\approx35.07$, so $g/\log p\approx32.3$ and $g/(\log p)^2\approx0.921$.

The ratio to $\log p$ grows without bound (Westzynthius), and in all computed data the ratio to $(\log p)^2$ has stayed below $1$, consistent with Cramér's conjecture; the gap of $1132$ is one of the largest relative to $(\log p)^2$ known. Of course data at this scale cannot distinguish $(\log p)^2$ from, say, $(\log p)^2\log\log p$.

blocks.title: Example 4: beating the trivial covering
blocks.body: Let $P=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13=30030$. The trivial choice (every residue class $0$) shows that $2,3,\dots,16$, fifteen consecutive integers, each share a factor with $P$. Find a longer run, and turn it into a prime gap.
blocks.solution:
A computer search over one period of residues modulo $30030$ finds that the longest run of consecutive integers each sharing a prime factor with $P$ has length $21$, for example $9440,9441,\dots,9460$. (In the language of the Jacobsthal function, every $22$ consecutive integers contain one coprime to $P$, and $22$ is best possible.) Each of these numbers exceeds $13$, so all are composite. Indeed $9439$ and $9461$ are prime, a gap of exactly $22$.

For comparison, the trivial run $2,\dots,16$ only gives that $30030k+2,\dots,30030k+16$ are composite. For the primes up to $11$ ($P=2310$) the best run has length $13$, for example $114,\dots,126$, against the trivial $11$ ($2,\dots,12$); here $113$ and $127$ are prime, which is the record gap $14$. As more primes are used the advantage of clever coverings over the trivial one grows, and quantifying that growth is exactly the Erdős–Rankin problem.

blocks.body:
- "Gaps are about $\log p$" is a statement about averages. Individual gaps are conjecturally spread out with an exponential distribution (Gallagher, assuming the Hardy–Littlewood prime tuple conjectures), and maximal gaps are of a different order.
- The factorial construction gives far smaller gaps relative to the size of the numbers than what actually occurs; do not use it to estimate $G(x)$.
- The Cramér model is a guide, not a theorem, and Maier's theorem shows it is wrong in detail.
- RH gives $g_n\ll\sqrt{p_n}\log p_n$, which is not enough for Legendre's conjecture.
- Numerical evidence (e.g. for primes of the form $n^2+1$) is not a proof; the parity problem is a genuine obstruction for sieve methods.

Everything here starts from the [[pnt|prime number theorem]]. Short intervals depend on zeros of $\zeta$ through [[zero-density|density estimates]] and the [[rh|Riemann hypothesis]]; long gaps depend on [[smooth-powerful|smooth numbers]], the [[crt|Chinese remainder theorem]] and coverings by residue classes ([[covering-systems]]). Small gaps lead to [[bounded-gaps]] and the [[twin-primes|twin prime conjecture]]; patterns in dense sets lead to [[arithmetic-progressions]] and the Green–Tao theorem; additive problems such as [[goldbach|Goldbach's conjecture]] are attacked with sieves and the [[circle-method|circle method]]. Random models of the primes belong to [[probabilistic-nt|probabilistic number theory]].

2. Using the prime number theorem, show that for every $\varepsilon>0$ the interval $(x,(1+\varepsilon)x]$ contains a prime for all large $x$.
3. Explain why Cramér's conjecture would imply Legendre's conjecture for all large $n$.
4. Show that among any $10$ consecutive integers at least one is coprime to $210=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7$. So for the primes up to $7$ the trivial covering of $2,\dots,10$ cannot be beaten, in contrast with Example 4.

blocks.body:
Pick an integer $n$ at random from $1,\dots,x$. Being divisible by $2$ happens with probability about $\frac12$, by $3$ with probability about $\frac13$, and by both with probability about $\frac16$: these events behave like independent coin flips. So the number of distinct prime factors $\omega(n)=\sum_{p\mid n}1$ is, morally, a sum of independent random variables, one for each prime, and probability theory predicts how it is distributed.

Probabilistic number theory makes this precise. Its flagship result, the Erdős–Kac theorem (1940), says that $\omega(n)$ obeys the central limit theorem: it is approximately normal with mean and variance $\log\log n$. The same viewpoint explains why the average of an arithmetic function can be very different from its typical value, and it supplies the random models used to make conjectures about primes.

blocks.title: Divisibility events are nearly independent
blocks.body:
For distinct primes $p_1,\dots,p_k$, by unique factorisation $n$ is divisible by all of them exactly when $p_1\cdots p_k\mid n$, so
$$\frac1x\#\{n\le x:\ p_1\mid n,\dots,p_k\mid n\}=\frac1x\Bigl\lfloor\frac{x}{p_1\cdots p_k}\Bigr\rfloor=\frac1{p_1}\cdots\frac1{p_k}+O\Bigl(\frac1x\Bigr).$$
So the indicator functions $\mathbf 1_{p\mid n}$ behave like independent Bernoulli random variables $X_p$ with $\Pr(X_p=1)=\frac1p$, as long as the product of the primes involved is small compared with $x$. The model breaks down for large primes: no $n\le x$ is divisible by two primes greater than $\sqrt x$, although the model would allow it.

In the model, $\omega$ corresponds to $\sum_{p\le x}X_p$ ([[random-variables]]), with mean $\sum_{p\le x}\frac1p$ and variance $\sum_{p\le x}\frac1p(1-\frac1p)$. By [[mertens|Mertens' theorem]], $\sum_{p\le x}\frac1p=\log\log x+M+O(1/\log x)$ with $M\approx0.2615$, so both are $\log\log x+O(1)$. The [[limit-theorems|central limit theorem]] then predicts that $(\omega(n)-\log\log x)/\sqrt{\log\log x}$ is approximately standard normal. The proof has to deal with the failure of independence for large primes.

blocks.title: Normal order
blocks.body:
An arithmetic function $f$ has normal order $F(n)$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$
$$\#\{n\le x:\ |f(n)-F(n)|>\varepsilon F(n)\}=o(x)\qquad(x\to\infty).$$
That is, for almost all $n$ (all but a set of density zero), $f(n)=(1+o(1))F(n)$. This describes the typical size of $f$, which need not match its average.

blocks.title: Hardy–Ramanujan theorem, with Turán's variance bound
blocks.body:
For $x\ge3$,
$$\sum_{n\le x}\bigl(\omega(n)-\log\log x\bigr)^2\ll x\log\log x.$$
Consequently $\omega(n)$ has normal order $\log\log n$ (Hardy and Ramanujan, 1917).

Write $L=\log\log x$ and use $\sum_{p\le x}\frac1p=L+O(1)$ and $\pi(x)=O(x/\log x)=O(x)$.

First moment. Swapping sums,
$$S_1=\sum_{n\le x}\omega(n)=\sum_{p\le x}\Bigl\lfloor\frac xp\Bigr\rfloor=x\sum_{p\le x}\frac1p+O(\pi(x))=xL+O(x).$$

Second moment. $\omega(n)^2=\sum_{p\mid n}\sum_{q\mid n}1$, counting ordered pairs of prime divisors. Pairs with $p=q$ give $\omega(n)$ again; pairs with $p\ne q$ need $pq\mid n$. So
$$S_2=\sum_{n\le x}\omega(n)^2=\sum_{\substack{p\ne q\\ pq\le x}}\Bigl\lfloor\frac x{pq}\Bigr\rfloor+S_1\le x\sum_{\substack{p,q\le x}}\frac1{pq}+S_1=x\Bigl(\sum_{p\le x}\frac1p\Bigr)^2+S_1=xL^2+O(xL).$$

Expanding the square,
$$\sum_{n\le x}(\omega(n)-L)^2=S_2-2LS_1+L^2\lfloor x\rfloor\le xL^2+O(xL)-2L\bigl(xL+O(x)\bigr)+xL^2=O(xL).$$

Normal order. By Chebyshev's inequality, for any $\varepsilon>0$ the number of $n\le x$ with $|\omega(n)-L|>\varepsilon L$ is at most $O(xL)/(\varepsilon L)^2=O\bigl(x/(\varepsilon^2L)\bigr)=o(x)$. To replace $L=\log\log x$ by $\log\log n$, note that for $\sqrt x<n\le x$ we have $\log\log x-\log2\le\log\log n\le\log\log x$, and the $n\le\sqrt x$ are only $o(x)$ of them.

blocks.title: Erdős–Kac theorem
blocks.body:
For every real $t$,
$$\frac1x\#\Bigl\{n\le x:\ \frac{\omega(n)-\log\log n}{\sqrt{\log\log n}}\le t\Bigr\}\to\Phi(t)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^te^{-s^2/2}\,ds\qquad(x\to\infty).$$
The same holds with $\omega$ replaced by $\Omega(n)$, the number of prime factors counted with multiplicity.

blocks.title: How the Erdős–Kac theorem is proved
blocks.body:
We sketch the method of moments; the details are omitted.

1. Truncate. Let $y=x^{\varepsilon(x)}$ with $\varepsilon(x)\to0$ slowly, and $\omega_y(n)=\#\{p\le y:\ p\mid n\}$. A number $n\le x$ has at most $1/\varepsilon(x)$ prime factors above $y$, so $\omega(n)-\omega_y(n)\le1/\varepsilon(x)$. If $\varepsilon(x)$ tends to $0$ slowly enough that $1/\varepsilon(x)=o(\sqrt{\log\log x})$, this difference does not affect the limit. Also $\sum_{y<p\le x}\frac1p=\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon(x)}+o(1)$ is $o(\sqrt{\log\log x})$, so the centring is unchanged.
2. Compare moments. For fixed $k$, expand $\sum_{n\le x}\bigl(\omega_y(n)-\mu_y\bigr)^k$, where $\mu_y=\sum_{p\le y}\frac1p$. It becomes a sum over $k$-tuples of primes $\le y$ of counts of $n\le x$ divisible by given products, which by the computation above equal the model probabilities up to errors $O(1)$ each. There are at most $\pi(y)^k\le y^k=x^{k\varepsilon(x)}$ tuples, so the total error is $o(x)$. Hence the $k$-th moment of $\omega_y(n)-\mu_y$ over $n\le x$ agrees asymptotically with that of $\sum_{p\le y}(X_p-\frac1p)$ for independent $X_p$.
3. Apply the CLT. The variance of the model sum tends to infinity and the summands are bounded, so the normalised model sum tends to the normal distribution, with convergence of all moments.
4. Conclude. The normal distribution is determined by its moments, so convergence of moments implies convergence in distribution for $\omega_y$, hence for $\omega$.

Kac's original heuristic and Erdős's sieve argument were combined in 1940; the moment proof above is due to later authors (Halberstam, Billingsley, and in a particularly clean form Granville and Soundararajan). Rényi and Turán showed that the rate of convergence is $O(1/\sqrt{\log\log x})$, which explains why the theorem is almost invisible in numerical data (Example 3).

blocks.title: Beyond ω: additive functions and random models
blocks.body:
A function $f$ is additive if $f(mn)=f(m)+f(n)$ whenever $\gcd(m,n)=1$. Both $\omega$ and $\log\frac{\varphi(n)}{n}=\sum_{p\mid n}\log(1-\frac1p)$ are additive, and the probabilistic model treats every additive function as a sum of nearly independent contributions $f(p^k)$ ([[arithmetic-functions]]). Two broad theorems:
- Erdős–Wintner: a real additive function has a limiting distribution if and only if the three series $\sum_{|f(p)|>1}\frac1p$, $\sum_{|f(p)|\le1}\frac{f(p)}p$ and $\sum_{|f(p)|\le1}\frac{f(p)^2}p$ all converge. For $f=\log\frac{\varphi(n)}n$ we have $f(p)\approx-\frac1p$, so all three converge, and $\frac{\varphi(n)}{n}$ has a limiting distribution (Schoenberg, 1928); its mean is $\frac6{\pi^2}$.
- When the series diverge, the distribution must be normalised; Kubilius developed a general theory of this case, in which Erdős–Kac is the model example and a central limit theorem holds under suitable conditions.

For the primes themselves, Cramér's model (each $n$ is "prime" independently with probability $1/\log n$) predicts the right density and is the source of conjectures on gaps ([[prime-patterns]]). It must be corrected for divisibility by small primes; the corrected version reproduces the Hardy–Littlewood prime tuple conjectures, including the constant in the [[twin-primes|twin prime]] asymptotic. Maier's theorem shows that even so, the model fails in very short intervals. Probabilistic heuristics are reliable guides only when the arithmetic correlations are put in by hand.

blocks.title: Example 1: the average of ω
blocks.body: Show that $\sum_{n\le x}\omega(n)=x\log\log x+Mx+O(x/\log x)$, and compare with the computed average for $x=10^6$.
blocks.solution:
As in the proof, $\sum_{n\le x}\omega(n)=\sum_{p\le x}\lfloor x/p\rfloor$. Writing $\lfloor x/p\rfloor=x/p-\{x/p\}$, the fractional parts contribute at most $\pi(x)=O(x/\log x)$, and Mertens' theorem gives $x\sum_{p\le x}\frac1p=x\log\log x+Mx+O(x/\log x)$.

For $x=10^6$: $\log\log x\approx2.626$, and the prediction for the average is $2.626+0.2615\approx2.887$. The actual average of $\omega(n)$ over $n\le10^6$ is $2.854$; the difference $0.033$ is within the $O(1/\log x)$ error, as $1/\log10^6\approx0.072$.

blocks.title: Example 2: typical versus average number of divisors
blocks.body: Show that $2^{\omega(n)}\le\tau(n)\le2^{\Omega(n)}$, and deduce that for almost all $n$, $\tau(n)=(\log n)^{\log2+o(1)}$. Compare with the average $\frac1x\sum_{n\le x}\tau(n)\sim\log x$.
blocks.solution:
If $n=\prod p_i^{e_i}$ then $\tau(n)=\prod(e_i+1)$, and $2\le e_i+1\le2^{e_i}$ for $e_i\ge1$. Multiplying over $i$ gives $2^{\omega(n)}\le\tau(n)\le2^{\Omega(n)}$.

By Hardy–Ramanujan (and the same argument for $\Omega$, whose average exceeds that of $\omega$ only by $O(1)$), for almost all $n$ both $\omega(n)$ and $\Omega(n)$ are $(1+o(1))\log\log n$. Then $\tau(n)$ is between $2^{(1+o(1))\log\log n}$ and the same with $\Omega$, i.e. $\tau(n)=(\log n)^{\log2+o(1)}$ with $\log2\approx0.693$.

So the typical $n$ has about $(\log n)^{0.69}$ divisors, but the average is $\log x$ ([[arithmetic-functions]]): a thin set of integers with very many divisors dominates the mean. At $x=10^6$ the mean of $\tau(n)$ is $13.97$ while the median is $8$; $(\log x)^{\log2}\approx6.2$.

blocks.title: Example 3: what the data look like at x = 10^6
blocks.body: Tabulate $\omega(n)$ for $n\le10^6$ and compare with the normal approximation of mean and variance $\log\log x\approx2.63$.
blocks.solution:
Counting gives: $\omega=0$ once ($n=1$), $\omega=1$ for $78734$ numbers, $2$ for $288726$, $3$ for $379720$, $4$ for $208034$, $5$ for $42492$, $6$ for $2285$ and $7$ for $8$. (No $n\le10^6$ has eight distinct prime factors, since $2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\cdot17\cdot19=9699690$.)

The mean is $2.85$, but the variance is only $0.98$, far below $2.63$. The reason is that $\omega$ is a sum of only a few effective "coins": the primes that can occur in an $n\le x$ have $\sum1/p$ about $2.9$, and the constraint that the product is at most $x$ creates strong negative correlations among large primes. As $\log\log x$ grows by $1$ only when $x$ is raised to the power $e$, the Gaussian shape emerges extremely slowly, in line with the Rényi–Turán rate $1/\sqrt{\log\log x}$. The theorem is true; it is just not something one sees on a computer.

blocks.title: Example 4: an exact identity behind 2^ω
blocks.body: Show that $2^{\omega(n)}=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)^2$, and deduce $\sum_{n\le x}2^{\omega(n)}=\sum_{d\le x}\mu(d)^2\lfloor x/d\rfloor$. Conclude that the average of $2^{\omega(n)}$ is of order $\log x$, much larger than its typical size $(\log x)^{\log2}$.
blocks.solution:
The squarefree divisors of $n$ are the products of subsets of the $\omega(n)$ distinct primes dividing $n$, so there are $2^{\omega(n)}$ of them, and $\mu(d)^2$ is the indicator that $d$ is squarefree. Summing over $n\le x$ and swapping the order: each squarefree $d\le x$ divides $\lfloor x/d\rfloor$ integers $n\le x$.

Since the squarefree numbers have density $\frac6{\pi^2}$ ([[smooth-powerful]]), partial summation gives $\sum_{d\le x}\mu(d)^2/d=\frac6{\pi^2}\log x+O(1)$, hence $\sum_{n\le x}2^{\omega(n)}=\frac6{\pi^2}x\log x+O(x)$. Numerically at $x=10^6$ the ratio $\frac{1}{x\log x}\sum_{n\le x}2^{\omega(n)}$ is $0.665$, approaching $\frac6{\pi^2}\approx0.608$ slowly because of the $O(x)$ term.

The typical value is $2^{(1+o(1))\log\log n}=(\log n)^{\log2+o(1)}$, so again the mean is dominated by a small set of $n$ with unusually many prime factors.

blocks.body:
- Typical is not average. $\tau(n)$ and $2^{\omega(n)}$ have averages of order $\log x$ but typical sizes $(\log n)^{0.69}$.
- The independence model holds only for small primes. Two primes above $\sqrt x$ cannot both divide $n\le x$, and ignoring this distorts variances (Example 3).
- Do not expect to see Erdős–Kac numerically. With $\log\log10^{100}\approx5.4$, even astronomically large $x$ give few effective coin flips.
- "Almost all" means all but a set of density zero; there are infinitely many exceptions, such as the primorials, with $\omega(n)\sim\log n/\log\log n$.
- Random models of the primes (Cramér) are heuristics. They need corrections for small primes and still fail in very short intervals (Maier).

The inputs are [[mertens|Mertens' theorems]] and the [[pnt|prime number theorem]], and the arithmetic functions studied are those of [[arithmetic-functions]]; the probability is the [[limit-theorems|law of large numbers and central limit theorem]] applied to sums of [[random-variables]]. Sieve methods ([[sieve-basics]]) are the tool for controlling the dependence between divisibility events, and the largest prime factor of a random integer, governed by Dickman's function, comes from [[smooth-powerful|smooth numbers]]. Random models of the primes generate the conjectures in [[prime-patterns]] and [[twin-primes]]. The same philosophy, that arithmetic quantities look like sums of independent random variables, appears in the distribution of values of $L$-functions and in the [[probabilistic-method|probabilistic method]] in combinatorics.

1. Show that $\sum_{n\le x}\Omega(n)-\sum_{n\le x}\omega(n)=O(x)$, so $\Omega$ also has normal order $\log\log n$.
2. Using Chebyshev's inequality and the variance bound, show that the proportion of $n\le x$ with $|\omega(n)-\log\log x|>(\log\log x)^{3/4}$ is $O((\log\log x)^{-1/2})$.
3. Show that the proportion of $n\le x$ with $\omega(n)=1$ tends to $0$, and identify its order of magnitude.
4. Show that $\frac1x\sum_{n\le x}\frac{\varphi(n)}n\to\frac6{\pi^2}$ by writing $\frac{\varphi(n)}n=\sum_{d\mid n}\frac{\mu(d)}d$.
